description: Language-neutral conformance scenarios consumed by the TypeScript and PHP test suites.

vectors.name: ordinary 2026 401k plan-term capacity
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 IRC 402(g)(1) elective-deferral limit at 24500 and the IRC 415(c)(1)(A) annual-additions dollar limit at 72000. With 200000 of compensation, the IRC 415(c)(1)(B) percentage limit does not bind. The stated 24500 deferral leaves 72000 - 24500 = 47500 that can be filled only if the plan terms permit employer or after-tax contributions, so that portion is determinate_with_assumptions.

vectors.name: 2026 high-wage age-60-to-63 Roth catch-up
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 IRC 402(g)(1) limit at 24500 and the SECURE 2.0 Act section 109 enhanced IRC 414(v) catch-up at 11250 for participants attaining ages 60 through 63. The prior-year FICA wages of 150001 exceed the 150000 IRC 414(v)(7) threshold published by that Notice, so the permitted 11250 catch-up is designated Roth under the SECURE 2.0 Act section 603 rule; 24500 + 11250 = 35750.

vectors.name: 2026 Roth IRA MFJ phaseout
vectors.description: IRC 408A(c)(3) reduces a Roth IRA contribution across the statutory phase-out range. Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 joint-return range at 242000 through 252000 and the under-50 IRC 219(b)(1) amount at 7500. At MAGI 247000, the reduction is 7500 x (247000 - 242000) / 10000 = 3750, leaving 7500 - 3750 = 3750 (already a multiple of the IRS worksheet's 10-dollar rounding increment).

vectors.name: shared traditional and Roth IRA pool
vectors.description: IRC 219(b)(1) permits one 7500 IRA contribution for this under-50 individual, and IRC 408A(c)(3) makes the Roth amount 7500 x (168000 - 158000) / (168000 - 153000) = 5000 using Notice 2025-67's 2026 single Roth range. IRC 219(b)(5) aggregates traditional and Roth IRA contributions, so the priority-one Roth allocation of 5000 leaves 7500 - 5000 = 2500 deductible traditional IRA capacity; the total remains 7500.

vectors.name: 401k and governmental 457b are separate
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets both the 2026 IRC 402(g)(1) elective-deferral limit and IRC 457(b)(2) governmental-plan limit at 24500. IRC 457(b) provides its own limit rather than sharing IRC 402(g), so each account receives 24500 and total employee pre-tax contributions are 24500 + 24500 = 49000.

vectors.name: mega backdoor 401k fills 415c
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 IRC 402(g)(1) deferral limit at 24500 and IRC 415(c)(1)(A) annual-additions limit at 72000. The supplied 10000 employer contribution plus the regular deferral use 34500, leaving 72000 - 24500 - 10000 = 37500 for plan-permitted after-tax employee contributions; all components sum to 72000.

vectors.name: self-employed solo 401k
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 gives a 24500 IRC 402(g)(1) deferral limit and a 72000 IRC 415(c)(1)(A) annual-additions limit. The IRC 401(c)(2) self-employed equivalent of a 25-percent employer rate is 20 percent, so 20 percent x 200000 = 40000 employer contribution. Plan-permitted after-tax contributions then fill 72000 - 24500 - 40000 = 7500.

vectors.name: 403b 15-year catch-up
vectors.description: IRC 402(g)(7)(C) limits the special 403(b) catch-up to the least of 3000, 15000 less prior special catch-up, and 5000 times years of service less prior elective deferrals. Here those are 3000, 15000, and (5000 x 15) - 20000 = 55000, so the special catch-up is 3000 in addition to Notice 2025-67's 24500 regular IRC 402(g) limit.

vectors.name: 457b special last-three-years catch-up
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 IRC 457(b)(2) base limit at 24500. IRC 457(b)(3) permits a special last-three-years total of the lesser of twice that limit (49000) and the base limit plus unused prior deferrals (24500 + 30000 = 54500), so the total is 49000; the special catch-up replaces rather than stacks with IRC 414(v) age catch-up. The regular 24500 plus the additional 24500 special component totals 49000.

vectors.name: 1994 historical employer-plan limits
vectors.description: The IRS Coda manual's historical table records the 1994 IRC 402(g) elective-deferral limit as 9240 and the IRC 415(c)(1)(A) dollar limit as 30000. IRC 415(c)(1)(B) then capped annual additions at 25 percent of compensation, and 25 percent x 100000 = 25000 is below the 30000 dollar limit, so the percentage limit binds and the stated statutory maximum is 25000.

vectors.name: 1985 employer-plan limit remains indeterminate
vectors.description: The repository's historical-coverage policy records that pre-1987 employer-plan limits cannot be reduced to one universal modern IRC 402(g)/415(c) value without plan-document and historical-law facts. The primary historical tables do not support inventing one for this 1985 account, so the statutory maximum is null and the prescribed result is indeterminate with HISTORICAL_415C_LIMIT_INDETERMINATE.

vectors.name: 1979 spousal IRA is indeterminate under the former IRC 220 twice-the-lesser rule
vectors.description: Former IRC 220(b)(1) (Tax Reform Act of 1976, Pub. L. 94-455 s.1501) allowed a one-earner couple the smallest of twice the amount paid to whichever account received the lesser amount, 15 percent of compensation, and $1,750. Subparagraph (A) makes the ceiling a joint figure keyed to how the couple split their contributions, not a cap on either account: a worker contributing nothing to their own account makes the spousal amount deductible only to zero, and the maximizing split is $875 to each. No single per-account number reproduces that, so the account reports no maximum and says why, rather than the $250 it once reported -- a figure matching no fact pattern, since a 1,500/250 split deducts only twice the lesser, or $500.

vectors.name: 1982 nonworking spouse IRA
vectors.description: ERTA 1981 rewrote IRC 219(c) for 1982: the spousal deduction is limited to the lesser of 2250 or compensation, reduced under 219(c)(2)(B) by the amount allowed as a deduction for the working spouse's own IRA, and in no event more than 2000 to the spousal account. The IRS SOI Bulletin for 1982 states the same rule: a 2250 one-earner total with no more than 2000 contributed to either spouse's IRA. The working spouse here contributes nothing to an IRA of their own, so the 219(c)(2)(B) subtraction is zero and the nonworking spouse's account may receive the full 2000; the 2250 household cap binds only the couple's combined total.

vectors.name: IRA conversion Form 8606 pro-rata
vectors.description: IRC 408(d)(2) and Form 8606 aggregate traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRAs for basis recovery. The conversion is 20000 and the denominator is 80000 year-end value plus 20000 distributed = 100000, so the nontaxable share is 20000 x 20000 / 100000 = 4000 and the taxable share is 20000 - 4000 = 16000. A conversion is not an IRC 219 contribution.

vectors.name: in-plan Roth rollover basis
vectors.description: IRC 402A(c)(4) treats an in-plan Roth rollover as taxable except for basis. Of the 50000 rolled over, the supplied 10000 after-tax basis is nontaxable, so 50000 - 10000 = 40000 is taxable.

vectors.name: 2026 enhanced SIMPLE
vectors.description: SECURE 2.0 Act section 117 raises the eligible SIMPLE plan's 2026 salary-reduction limit to 18100, as published in Notice 2025-67. Section 109's enhanced IRC 414(v) catch-up at age 61 is 5250. The mandatory SIMPLE match is 3 percent of 100000 = 3000 under IRC 408(p)(2)(A)(ii), so 18100 + 5250 + 3000 = 26350.

vectors.name: cash-balance contribution is actuarial
vectors.description: A cash-balance plan is a defined-benefit plan; its funding contribution depends on the actuarial valuation required by IRC 412 and 430 rather than the defined-contribution IRC 415(c) annual-additions limit. No valuation or plan-benefit facts are supplied, so no universal maximum can be derived and the result is indeterminate with the actuarial-valuation diagnostic.

vectors.name: self-employed retirement deduction classification
vectors.description: IRC 404(a)(8) allows the deductible self-employed retirement contribution, while a sole proprietor has no Form W-2 wage reduction. Notice 2025-67 supplies 24500 under IRC 402(g); the IRC 401(c)(2) equivalent employer rate yields 20 percent x 200000 = 40000. Thus the above-the-line deduction and AGI reduction are 24500 + 40000 = 64500, and the W-2 box 1 reduction is zero.

vectors.name: 2009 MFS living apart Roth conversion
vectors.description: Before 2010, IRC 408A(c)(3)(B) barred conversions above 100000 MAGI and for MFS taxpayers, but an MFS taxpayer who did not live with a spouse during the year is treated under the applicable IRA rules as single for that restriction. MAGI 90000 therefore permits the conversion. IRC 408(d)(2)'s denominator is 10000 ending value plus 10000 converted = 20000, so 10000 x 10000 / 20000 = 5000 basis and 5000 taxable.

vectors.name: SIMPLE additional nonelective 10 percent cap
vectors.description: SECURE 2.0 Act section 117 permits the additional SIMPLE nonelective contribution but caps it at the lesser of 10 percent of compensation and the indexed dollar cap. Ten percent of 20000 is 2000, below Notice 2025-67's 5300 cap; with the mandatory 2-percent contribution of 400 under IRC 408(p)(2)(A)(iii), employer contributions are 2000 + 400 = 2400. The statutory maximum is the 17000 salary reduction plus 2600 permitted employer amount, or 19600.

vectors.name: SIMPLE IRA Roth catch-up wage-test exclusion
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 SIMPLE salary-reduction limit at 17000 and the age-60-to-63 catch-up at 5250. SECURE 2.0 Act section 603's mandatory-Roth rule applies only when prior-year FICA wages exceed the indexed threshold; no employer wage record is supplied, so it cannot require Roth treatment. The permitted components are therefore 17000 pre-tax deferral, 5250 pre-tax catch-up, and zero Roth catch-up.

vectors.name: aggregate 403b 15-year catch-up pool
vectors.description: IRC 402(g)(7) is an aggregate per-individual 403(b) special-catch-up limit, not a separate 3000 entitlement for each contract. Each account's facts independently produce the 3000 least-of amount, but the priority-one account consumes the entire 3000 shared pool, leaving zero for the priority-two account.

vectors.name: pre-2023 Roth employer contribution unavailable
vectors.description: SECURE 2.0 Act section 604 first permitted participants to elect designated Roth treatment for vested employer matching and nonelective contributions, effective after enactment. The 2022 contribution predates that authority, so no employer Roth amount can be derived; the 2022 IRC 402(g) regular deferral remains 20500 and the result is indeterminate with the availability diagnostic.

vectors.name: aggregate IRA conversion basis penny allocation
vectors.description: IRC 408(d)(2) applies one aggregate basis fraction: 1 of basis over 147 year-end value plus 3 converted = 1/150. The three 1-dollar conversions therefore recover 3/150 = 0.02 of basis in total; cents rounding allocates the two pennies deterministically to the first two conversions, leaving 2.98 taxable in total.

vectors.name: 1997 SEP formula applies 401a17 compensation ceiling before 15 percent rate
vectors.description: For 1997, IRC 401(a)(17)'s indexed compensation ceiling is 160000 and the IRS SEP/SARSEP audit guidance applies the plan's 15-percent rate to capped compensation. Thus 15 percent x 160000 = 24000. That is below the IRC 415(c) dollar limit, so the statutory maximum, employer contribution, and input-based maximum are all 24000.

vectors.name: 1997 nonelective formula applies 401a17 compensation ceiling
vectors.description: IRC 415(c)(1) gives a 1997 annual-additions maximum of the lesser of 30000 and 25 percent of compensation; 25 percent x 500000 = 125000, so the statutory maximum is 30000. IRC 401(a)(17)'s 160000 compensation cap applies before the supplied 15-percent employer formula, producing 15 percent x 160000 = 24000 for both the contribution and input-based maximum.

vectors.name: 1997 self-employed SEP uses reduced-rate and capped plan-rate worksheet ceilings
vectors.description: The IRS self-employed SEP worksheet reduces a 15-percent plan rate to 15 / 115 = 13.043478 percent for net earnings: that rate times 500000 exceeds the separate 15 percent x 160000 = 24000 capped-plan-rate ceiling under IRC 401(a)(17). The 1997 IRC 415(c) dollar ceiling is higher, so all asserted contribution maxima are 24000.

vectors.name: 1997 self-employed qualified plan applies reduced-rate and capped plan-rate ceilings
vectors.description: The IRS self-employed qualified-plan worksheet reduces the 15-percent plan rate to 15 / 115 = 13.043478 percent of 500000 net earnings, but IRC 401(a)(17)'s 160000 compensation ceiling also makes the plan-rate ceiling 15 percent x 160000 = 24000. IRC 415(c)'s 30000 dollar limit is higher, so the employer contribution and input-based maximum are 24000 while the statutory maximum is 30000.

vectors.name: 1998 SEP compensation below 400 reports maximum-excludable threshold
vectors.description: Notice 97-58 sets the 1998 IRC 408(k)(2)(C) SEP compensation amount at 400. With plan compensation of 399, the calculation remains determinate because the statute permits rather than mandates exclusion, but it must report the plan-document-dependent below-threshold warning. This vector fails before the sourced 400 value is encoded because the warning is absent.

vectors.name: 2005 designated Roth governmental 457b unavailable
vectors.description: The Pension Protection Act of 2006 section 827 extended IRC 402A designated Roth treatment to governmental IRC 457(b) plans only for taxable years beginning after 2010. A 2005 designated Roth governmental 457(b) account therefore has no statutory availability or contribution capacity, yielding unavailable and zero.

vectors.name: 2011 first-year designated Roth governmental 457b
vectors.description: Pension Protection Act of 2006 section 827 made designated Roth governmental IRC 457(b) contributions available for taxable years beginning after 2010. Notice 2010-95 sets the 2011 IRC 457(b)(2) limit at 16500, so the first eligible year's Roth deferral and maximum are both 16500.

vectors.name: 2025 SIMPLE 401k match capped by 401a17 compensation
vectors.description: Notice 2024-80 sets the 2025 SIMPLE salary-reduction limit at 16500 and IRC 401(a)(17) compensation cap at 350000. A SIMPLE 401(k)'s 3-percent match is therefore 3 percent x 350000 = 10500, not 3 percent of 500000; together with 16500, the maximum is 27000.

vectors.name: 2025 SIMPLE IRA match exempt from 401a17 compensation cap
vectors.description: Notice 2024-80 sets the 2025 SIMPLE salary-reduction limit at 16500. IRC 408(p)(2)(A)(ii) bases a SIMPLE IRA's 3-percent match on the employee's compensation and does not import the qualified-plan IRC 401(a)(17) compensation limit, so 3 percent x 500000 = 15000. The maximum is 16500 + 15000 = 31500.

vectors.name: 2026 MFS living together Roth IRA phase-out
vectors.description: IRC 408A(c)(3) supplies a separate 0 through 10000 phase-out for a married-filing-separately individual who lived with a spouse. Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 under-50 contribution amount at 7500. At MAGI 5000, the reduction is 7500 x 5000 / 10000 = 3750, leaving a 3750 Roth contribution after worksheet rounding.

vectors.name: 2026 MFS living together covered traditional IRA deduction phase-out
vectors.description: IRC 219(g) gives a covered married-filing-separately individual living with a spouse the 0 through 10000 deduction phase-out. Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 IRA contribution limit at 7500. At MAGI 5000, the deductible amount is 7500 - (7500 x 5000 / 10000) = 3750; IRC 219 permits the remaining 3750 contribution but not its deduction, so it is nondeductible and the total remains 7500.

vectors.name: 2026 modern spousal IRA from joint compensation
vectors.description: IRC 219(c) lets a joint-return couple use the other spouse's compensation after accounting for that spouse's IRA contribution. The taxpayer's 100000 compensation is more than the Notice 2025-67 2026 under-50 limit of 7500, so the non-earning spouse may make and deduct the full 7500 traditional IRA contribution.

vectors.name: 2026 noncovered spouse deduction phase-out band
vectors.description: IRC 219(g)(7) applies the noncovered spouse's joint-return deduction phase-out when the other spouse is covered. Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 band at 242000 through 252000 and the contribution amount at 7500. At MAGI 244000, the reduction is 7500 x 2000 / 10000 = 1500, leaving 6000 deductible and 1500 nondeductible contribution capacity.

vectors.name: 2026 ordinary age-50 catch-up at age 56
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 sets the 2026 IRC 402(g)(1) regular limit at 24500 and IRC 414(v) catch-up at 8000. SECURE 2.0's enhanced amount applies only to participants attaining ages 60 through 63, so an individual attaining 56 receives the ordinary 8000 catch-up and 24500 + 8000 = 32500 total.

vectors.name: 2026 age-64 reversion from enhanced catch-up
vectors.description: SECURE 2.0 Act section 109 limits the enhanced IRC 414(v) catch-up to participants attaining ages 60, 61, 62, or 63. An individual attaining 64 instead receives Notice 2025-67's ordinary 8000 catch-up; with the 24500 IRC 402(g)(1) limit, the maximum is 32500.

vectors.name: 2023 first-year Roth employer contribution
vectors.description: SECURE 2.0 Act section 604 permitted participants to elect designated Roth treatment for vested employer matching and nonelective contributions after enactment. Notice 2022-55 sets the 2023 IRC 402(g)(1) limit at 22500. The supplied 10000 employer contribution is therefore Roth, and 22500 + 10000 = 32500 maximum annual contribution based on the supplied plan terms.

vectors.name: 2010 Roth conversion after MAGI repeal
vectors.description: The Tax Increase Prevention and Reconciliation Act of 2005 repealed the IRC 408A(c)(3)(B) 100000 MAGI conversion restriction for tax years beginning after 2009, so MAGI 500000 does not bar this 2010 conversion. IRC 408(d)(2)'s basis fraction is 2000 / (8000 ending value + 2000 conversion) = 20 percent; 20 percent x 2000 = 400 nontaxable and 1600 taxable.

vectors.name: 2020 traditional IRA contribution after age-70-half repeal
vectors.description: SECURE Act section 114 repealed IRC 219(d)(1)'s age-70-and-one-half bar for contributions made for tax years beginning after 2019. The individual has 20000 compensation, exceeding the 2020 IRC 219(b) under-50 limit of 6000 plus 1000 IRC 219(b)(5) catch-up, so the age-72 taxpayer may deduct the full 7000.

vectors.name: 1975 first-year traditional IRA fifteen percent limit
vectors.description: Former IRC 219(b), as enacted for the first generally available IRA year, limited the deductible contribution to the lesser of 1500 or 15 percent of compensation. Fifteen percent x 20000 = 3000, so the 1500 statutory dollar limit binds and is fully deductible.

vectors.name: unsupported tax year 1974
vectors.description: The canonical statutory-parameter dataset begins at 1975, its first supported tax year; 1974 has no encoded primary-authority row. The input is therefore rejected with UNSUPPORTED_TAX_YEAR rather than extrapolating a retirement-law value.

vectors.name: duplicate account id
vectors.description: Account IDs identify accounts for allocation and conversion references, so the input contract requires them to be unique. The two supplied accounts both use a, making DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT_ID the required validation result before any statutory contribution calculation.

vectors.name: unknown account owner
vectors.description: An account's ownerId must name an entry in persons so that the account can be assigned that person's statutory limits. The supplied ownerId missing has no matching person, so the input contract requires UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT_OWNER before calculation.

vectors.name: negative compensation is invalid money
vectors.description: Compensation is a nonnegative monetary input used by IRC 219, 401, and 415 limits. The supplied -1 cannot be a valid amount under the library's money-input contract, so it is rejected as INVALID_MONEY rather than treated as a statutory negative limit.

vectors.name: invalid filing status alias
vectors.description: Filing status selects statutory IRA phase-out bands and spousal rules. XX is not one of the supported tax filing-status codes, so the input contract rejects it with INVALID_FILING_STATUS rather than mapping it to a legally different status.

vectors.name: 2026 full-year self-only HSA limit
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(1)-(2)(A): twelve eligible months each limited to one twelfth of the $4,400 self-only amount (Rev. Proc. 2025-19), so 12 x 4400 / 12 = 4400. Under 55, so no IRC 223(b)(3) increase.

vectors.name: 2026 full-year family HSA limit
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(2)(B): twelve eligible months of family coverage at one twelfth of $8,750 each, so 12 x 8750 / 12 = 8750. An unmarried individual with family coverage is not subject to the IRC 223(b)(5) division, so no share is recorded.

vectors.name: 2026 mid-year HSA coverage change prorated by month
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(2) sets a separate monthly limitation for each month, determined by the coverage held on that month's first day. Ineligible January and February contribute nothing; March through June are self-only at 4400/12; July through December are family at 8750/12. (4 x 4400 + 6 x 8750) / 12 = 70100 / 12 = 5841.67.

vectors.name: 2026 both spouses age 55 receive separate HSA catch-ups
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5) gives the couple one $8,750 family limit, divided equally by default at 4375 each. IRC 223(b)(3) adds $1,000 for each spouse who attains 55 before the close of the year, is excluded from the family division by IRC 223(b)(5)(B), and must go into that spouse's own HSA. Each account is therefore 4375 + 1000 = 5375 and the couple's total is 8750 + 2000 = 10750.

vectors.name: 2026 spouses divide the single family HSA limit as agreed
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides the one $8,750 family limit as the spouses agree. A 75/25 agreement yields 6562.50 and 2187.50, which still sum to exactly one family limit. Both spouses are under 55, so there is no IRC 223(b)(3) increase.

vectors.name: 2026 HSA last-month rule with a satisfied testing period
vectors.description: Eligible only in December. The ordinary IRC 223(b)(2) limitation is 4400 / 12 = 366.67. IRC 223(b)(8)(A) instead treats the individual as eligible for every month of 2026 with December's self-only coverage, giving the full 4400. The amount that could not have been contributed but for that rule is 4400 - 366.67 = 4033.33, and the IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(iii) testing period runs the thirteen months ending 2027-12. It is satisfied here, so nothing is included.

vectors.name: 2026 HSA last-month rule failed in the testing period
vectors.description: Same facts as the satisfied case, but the individual ceases to be an eligible individual inside the thirteen-month testing period. IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i)(I) includes the 4033.33 attributable to the rule in gross income for 2027, and (i)(II) adds a 10 percent additional tax of 403.33. Both fall in 2027, so the 2026 IRC 223(a) deduction is still the full 4400.

vectors.name: 2005 HSA monthly limit capped by the plan annual deductible
vectors.description: Before the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303, IRC 223(b)(2)(A) limited each month to one twelfth of the lesser of the plan's annual deductible and the dollar amount. For 2005 the self-only dollar amount is 2650 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71), so an 1800 deductible binds and the full-year limit is 1800. The individual attains 55 in 2005, so the non-indexed IRC 223(b)(3)(B) table adds 600.

vectors.name: 2006 HSA monthly limit capped by the statutory dollar amount
vectors.description: The same pre-2007 lesser-of test with the other branch binding: a 6000 family deductible exceeds the 2006 family dollar amount of 5450 (Rev. Proc. 2005-70), so the limit is 5450. IRC 223(b)(8) did not exist until taxable years beginning after 2006, so electing the last-month rule produces a diagnostic and the ordinary month-by-month limitation.

vectors.name: 2005 married couple with family coverage and no stated annual deductible leaves the IRC 223(b)(5) household limit indeterminate
vectors.description: Before the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303, IRC 223(b)(2)(A) limited each month to one twelfth of the lesser of the plan's annual deductible and the dollar amount, so the deductible is an operand of the limitation itself and not a refinement of it. The taxpayer supplies hdhpAnnualDeductible as null, which every money input in this package reads as the fact not being stated, and the spouse states no deductible either; neither operand of "the lesser of" is therefore known and no month has a determinable limitation. The 2005 family dollar amount of 5250 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71) is not the answer on its own, because IRC 223(b)(2)(A) reaches it only after the comparison. IRC 223(b)(5)(A) builds the one family limitation out of the spouses' own refigured limitations, so it is no more determinable than they are: the IRC 223(b)(1), 223(b)(5) and 223(b)(3) pools all report null rather than a ceiling the statute does not support. Reporting the uncompared dollar amount instead would overstate the ceiling, which is the direction that costs a taxpayer the IRC 4973 excise.

vectors.name: 2004 married couple with family coverage and no stated annual deductible leaves the IRC 223(b)(5) household limit indeterminate
vectors.description: The sibling year, pinned so the IRC 223(b)(2) era is covered at both ends rather than at one. IRC 223(b)(2)(A) applies for every year the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303 had not yet reached, which is 2004 through 2006, so the answer cannot turn on which of those years is asked about. The 2004 family dollar amount is 5150 (Rev. Proc. 2003-102) against 5250 for 2005, and with no annual deductible stated by either spouse neither figure is reachable: IRC 223(b)(2)(A) takes the lesser of the deductible and the dollar amount, and one operand is unknown. All three pools report null, as in 2005.

vectors.name: 2005 married couple with family coverage under two plans takes the lower annual deductible and stays determinate
vectors.description: The positive control for the two vectors above: the same shape with the deductibles actually stated must still produce a number, so that requiring the fact does not turn every pre-2007 couple indeterminate. IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats spouses with family coverage under different plans as covered by the plan with the lowest annual deductible, so 3000 governs rather than the spouse's 4000. IRC 223(b)(2)(A) then limits each month to one twelfth of the lesser of that 3000 and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71), giving 250 a month and 12 x 250 = 3000 for the year. Only one spouse holds a health savings account, so the whole family limitation is allocated to it under IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii). That allocation is an assumption about the division the spouses agreed on -- the statutory default absent an agreement is an equal division -- so the status is determinate_with_assumptions rather than determinate, even though every figure is determinable. The taxpayer attains 35 in 2005, so the IRC 223(b)(3) additional contribution amount does not apply and the statutory maximum is 3000.

vectors.name: 2005 a spouse's self-only deductible does not lower the IRC 223(b)(5) family limitation
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) reaches the lowest annual deductible only "if such spouses each have family coverage under different plans". Here only the taxpayer has family coverage; the spouse's own coverage is self-only, so the spouse has no family plan and the 1000 deductible of that self-only plan is not a candidate. The couple's family limitation is the deductible of a family plan, not of whatever plan is cheapest in the household. IRC 223(b)(2)(A) therefore takes the lesser of the taxpayer's 5000 family deductible and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71), giving 5000 rather than 1000. Note that IRC 223(b)(5)(A) separately treats the spouse as having the taxpayer's family coverage, which is why the spouse's self-only months do not produce a self-only portion; being treated as having family coverage is not the same as having a family plan whose deductible competes.

vectors.name: 2005 two family plans take the lower annual deductible under IRC 223(b)(5)(A)
vectors.description: The companion to the vector above, holding everything else constant so the two differ only in the spouse's coverage tier. Both spouses have family coverage under different plans, which is exactly the condition IRC 223(b)(5)(A) states for treating them as covered under the plan with the lowest annual deductible, so the spouse's 3000 competes and wins against the taxpayer's 5000. IRC 223(b)(2)(A) then takes the lesser of 3000 and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250, giving 3000. Read against the self-only vector this pins the distinction the statute draws: a family plan's deductible competes and a self-only plan's does not.

vectors.name: 2005 a family-covered spouse who omits their annual deductible leaves the family limitation indeterminate
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats spouses who each have family coverage under different plans as covered by the plan with the lowest annual deductible, so the couple's limitation turns on the least of their family-plan deductibles. Here the spouse states family coverage and no deductible for it. That plan could be the lower of the two, so the least is unknown and IRC 223(b)(2)(A)'s "lesser of the plan's annual deductible and the dollar amount" has an unknown operand; the taxpayer's own 5000 is not the answer merely because it is the only one supplied. Dropping the spouse from the comparison because their figure is absent would state a ceiling on facts that do not support it, and would overstate it whenever the spouse's plan is lower -- the direction that costs a taxpayer the IRC 4973 excise. Both the IRC 223(b)(5) pool and hsa.sharedFamilyContributionLimit, which is that same limitation reported per owner, therefore report null rather than the uncompared 5250 family dollar amount for 2005 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71).

vectors.name: 2005 one spouse's conflicting coverage facts leave the other spouse's share of the family limitation indeterminate
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives spouses who have family coverage a single family limitation, and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides that one limitation between them, so each spouse's share is a function of facts belonging to both. Here the taxpayer's own coverage is perfectly coherent -- family, 5000 deductible -- while the spouse holds two health savings accounts stating contradictory coverage, family at 3000 and self-only at 1000. Coverage is one fact about a person, so the spouse's is undeterminable, and with it the couple's single family limitation. The taxpayer's share of an undeterminable limitation is undeterminable too: having coherent facts of one's own does not make the couple's shared amount knowable. Every account drawing on that limitation therefore reports indeterminate with a null statutory maximum, a null IRC 223(b)(5) pool and a null sharedFamilyContributionLimit. Reporting a number for the taxpayer would be worse than merely wrong: it would be half of a figure taken from the very spouse whose facts contradict each other.

vectors.name: 2005 a spouse's family plan sets the deductible only for the months that plan was in force
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(2) builds the year out of twelve monthly limitations, each one twelfth of the lesser of the annual deductible and the dollar amount for the coverage in force that month, so the IRC 223(b)(5)(A) lowest-deductible comparison is answered per month and not once for the year. The taxpayer holds family coverage all year with a 5000 deductible; the spouse takes family coverage in December only, with a 1000 deductible. For January through November the taxpayer is the only spouse with a family plan, so each month uses the lesser of 5000 and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71), which is 5000. December has two family plans, so it uses the lesser of 1000 and 5250, which is 1000. The year is therefore (11 x 5000 + 1 x 1000) / 12 = 56000 / 12 = 4666.67. Applying the December plan's deductible to months in which the spouse held no family plan at all would understate the limitation by more than 3600, and is what a single whole-year comparison does.

vectors.name: 2005 an omitted annual deductible and an explicit null are the same fact
vectors.description: The normalization half of the pre-2007 fix, stated as a vector rather than left to the type system. Every money input in this package reads null as the fact not being stated -- money() returns the default for null and for an absent property alike -- so supplying hdhpAnnualDeductible as null and omitting the property must reach the identical result. This vector omits it entirely; the explicit-null vector supplies it as null; both are indeterminate with all three pools null. Telling the two apart is what produced the original TypeScript/PHP divergence, where a retained null reached Math.min as a zero and read as a deductible binding at nothing.

vectors.name: 2007 no annual deductible is required once the IRC 223(b)(2) cap is repealed
vectors.description: The effective-date boundary control for the three indeterminate vectors. Section 303 of the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 struck the IRC 223(b)(2)(A) comparison with the plan's annual deductible for taxable years beginning after 2006, so from 2007 the monthly limitation is one twelfth of the statutory amount alone and the deductible is not an operand of anything. The identical input that is indeterminate for 2005 must therefore be determinable for 2007: the family dollar amount is 5650 (Rev. Proc. 2006-53), the couple has family coverage for the whole year, and no deductible-required diagnostic is issued. This is what stops the fix from over-reaching into years the cap never governed.

vectors.name: a missing birth year leaves the IRC 223(b)(5) household limit determinable
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b)(5) household pool reports null only when the family limitation itself cannot be determined, not whenever anything about an owner is unknown. A missing birth year makes the IRC 223(b)(3) additional contribution amount for an individual who attains age 55 unknowable, so the account is indeterminate and its statutory maximum is null; but the family limitation is a function of coverage and the year alone, and for 2026 it is the full 8750 family amount (Rev. Proc. 2025-19) with both spouses covered all year. Reporting null for the shared pool here would discard a limit the statute does fix, and would make the audit trail less informative than the facts allow. The IRC 223(b)(3) pool, which is the one the missing fact actually reaches, is null.

vectors.name: 2026 employer HSA contribution is excluded rather than deducted
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b) ceiling is a single 4400. An employer or cafeteria-plan contribution of 1000 is excluded from gross income under IRC 106(d) and reduces the IRC 223(a) deduction under IRC 223(b)(4)(B), leaving 3400 deductible. The excluded 1000 is outside Form W-2 box 1 and outside Social Security and Medicare wages.

vectors.name: 2003 predates IRC 223 health savings accounts
vectors.description: IRC 223 was added by the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 section 1201, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2003. There is no 2003 limitation to prorate, so the account is unavailable rather than assigned an invented amount.

vectors.name: 2026 HSA last-month rule with an unresolved testing period
vectors.description: Eligible only in November and December, so the ordinary IRC 223(b)(2) limitation is 2 x 4400 / 12 = 733.33 and IRC 223(b)(8)(A) raises it to 4400. 4400 - 733.33 = 3666.67 could not have been contributed but for the rule. Whether the thirteen-month testing period is satisfied was not supplied, so compliance is not assumed: the result is determinate_with_assumptions and the 10 percent IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i)(II) tax of 366.67 is quantified rather than ignored.

vectors.name: 2026 married filing separately family coverage recharacterizes the other spouse
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats both spouses as having only family coverage for any month in which either has it, and IRC 223(b)(5) applies to individuals married to each other whether they file jointly or separately. The self-only spouse is therefore recharacterized to twelve family months, the couple shares one 8750 limit divided equally at 4375, and each spouse adds an IRC 223(b)(3) 1000 in that spouse's own account, for 5375 each and 10750 in total.

vectors.name: 2026 spouse family and self-only months divide only the family portion
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides only the limitation attributable to family-coverage months (Form 8889 line 6, Steps 1-4). The taxpayer has six family months and six self-only months while the spouse has six family months. Only the 6 x 8750 / 12 = 4375 family portion is divided equally; the taxpayer keeps the undivided 6 x 4400 / 12 = 2200 of self-only months, so the limits are 2187.50 + 2200 = 4387.50 and 2187.50.

vectors.name: 2026 spouses with unequal family-coverage months each divide their own refigured family limit
vectors.description: Form 8889 line 6 has each spouse refigure the limitation for the months that spouse was treated as having family coverage (Step 1) and divide that refigured amount (Steps 2-3). The refigured amount is therefore per spouse, not one couple-wide figure: the taxpayer's twelve family months refigure to 8750 and the spouse's six refigure to 6 x (8750/12) = 4375. An equal division gives the taxpayer 8750 x 1/2 = 4375 and the spouse 4375 x 1/2 = 2187.50. The spouse's limit is not raised to the taxpayer's share, so the couple's total is 6562.50, not 8750.

vectors.name: 2026 married last-month rule measures the attributable amount against the divided limit
vectors.description: Both spouses are eligible with family coverage only in December and elect IRC 223(b)(8). Each spouse's ceiling is an equal share of the family limit, 8750 / 2 = 4375. Without the last-month rule the same division would have applied to the one-month limitation, giving 1/2 x 8750/12 = 364.58, so the amount attributable to the rule under IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i) is 4375 - 364.58 = 4010.42 per spouse, with a 10 percent additional tax of 401.04 on failure.

vectors.name: 2026 spouse family coverage without an HSA recharacterizes the taxpayer's self-only months
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) applies when "either spouse" has family coverage; it does not ask whether that spouse owns a health savings account, so persons[].hsaCoverage carries the fact. The spouse has family coverage for all twelve months, so the taxpayer's twelve self-only months are treated as family months. Rev. Proc. 2025-19 sets the 2026 family amount at 8750, so IRC 223(b)(2)(B) gives 12 x (8750/12) = 8750. Only the taxpayer has an HSA, so the IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) division allocates the single family limit to it in full.

vectors.name: 2026 unstated spouse coverage leaves a self-only HSA limit indeterminate
vectors.description: The same scenario with the spouse's coverage unstated. IRC 223(b)(5)(A) makes the answer depend on a fact the input does not carry: family coverage held by the spouse yields 8750 and no family coverage yields the IRC 223(b)(2)(A) self-only figure of 12 x (4400/12) = 4400. The engine calculates statutory parameters from caller-supplied facts, so an unsupplied fact that changes the answer is indeterminate rather than assumed away.

vectors.name: 2026 spouse without high deductible coverage leaves the self-only HSA limit intact
vectors.description: An empty persons[].hsaCoverage records that the spouse held no high deductible health plan coverage in any month, so IRC 223(b)(5)(A) has nothing to recharacterize. The taxpayer's twelve self-only months give 12 x (4400/12) = 4400 under IRC 223(b)(2)(A) with the 2026 self-only amount from Rev. Proc. 2025-19, and no family limit is shared.

vectors.name: 2026 unmarried Archer MSA contribution reduces the HSA limit under IRC 223(b)(4)(A)
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces "the limitation which would (but for this paragraph) apply under this subsection" by "(A) the aggregate amount paid for such taxable year to Archer MSAs of such individual". Twelve self-only months give 12 x (4400/12) = 4400 under IRC 223(b)(2)(A) with the 2026 amount from Rev. Proc. 2025-19; the $1,200 paid to Archer MSAs reduces it to 4400 - 1200 = 3200. The individual is unmarried, so IRC 223(b)(5) does not apply and the IRC 223(b)(4) flush text does not withdraw subparagraph (A).

vectors.name: 2026 married Archer MSA reduction is taken before the IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) division
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b)(4) flush text says "Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any individual to whom paragraph (5) applies", so a married individual with family coverage routes through IRC 223(b)(5)(B), whose limitation "(i) shall be reduced by the aggregate amount paid to Archer MSAs of such spouses for the taxable year, and (ii) after such reduction, shall be divided equally between them". The 2026 family limitation from Rev. Proc. 2025-19 is 8750; both spouses' Archer contributions aggregate to 2000 + 1000 = 3000; 8750 - 3000 = 5750 is divided equally, giving each spouse 2875. Dividing first and reducing afterwards would give 4375 - 3000 = 1375 each and would subtract the aggregate twice, which is why the ordering is pinned here.

vectors.name: 2026 IRC 223(b)(4)(A) reduces the whole subsection (b) limitation including the age 55 amount
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces the limitation "under this subsection", not under paragraph (1), so it reaches the IRC 223(b)(3) increase as well. An unmarried individual aged 55 or over with twelve family-coverage months has 8750 + 1000 = 9750 for 2026; $9,000 paid to Archer MSAs leaves 750. The IRC 223(b)(1) limitation absorbs 8750 and the remaining 250 comes off the additional contribution amount, leaving 1000 - 250 = 750. hsa.additionalContributionAmount reports the unreduced IRC 223(b)(3) figure of 1000.

vectors.name: 2026 IRC 223(b)(5)(B) leaves the age 55 additional contribution amount untouched
vectors.description: Same person and same $9,000 paid to Archer MSAs as the unmarried case, but married to a spouse who has family coverage, so IRC 223(b)(5) applies and the IRC 223(b)(4) flush text withdraws subparagraph (A). IRC 223(b)(5)(B) reduces the limitation "under paragraph (1) ... without regard to any additional contribution amount under paragraph (3)", so only 8750 is exposed: 8750 - 9000 floors at 0, and the IRC 223(b)(3) amount of 1000 survives in full. The answer is 1000 rather than the 750 the same facts produce under IRC 223(b)(4)(A), which is exactly what the flush text does.

vectors.name: 2026 Archer MSA contribution above the HSA limit reduces it to zero, never below
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces the limitation "(but not below zero)". Twelve self-only months give 4400 for 2026 and the individual is under 55, so there is no IRC 223(b)(3) amount to absorb the rest; $5,000 paid to Archer MSAs takes the limitation to 0 rather than -600. The reduction actually absorbed is therefore 4400, not the 5000 paid.

vectors.name: 2026 Archer MSA reduction follows the IRC 223(b)(8) last-month rule
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(8)(A) applies "for purposes of computing the limitation under paragraph (1)", and IRC 223(b)(4) then reduces "the limitation which would (but for this paragraph) apply under this subsection" — so the reduction is taken after the last-month rule, not before. December-only self-only coverage with the election gives the full 4400 for 2026; 4400 - 1000 paid to Archer MSAs is 3400. The counterfactual month-by-month limitation is 4400/12 = 366.67, which the same $1,000 reduces to 0, so the amount that "could not have been made but for" IRC 223(b)(8)(A) under IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i)(I) is the whole 3400 rather than 3400 - 366.67. hsa.contributionLimitWithoutLastMonthRule reports the unreduced 366.67 counterfactual.

vectors.name: persons entry that is not an object is rejected
vectors.description: A non-object entry in persons has no id, but reporting it as a missing id hides the real defect and diverged between the two engines. Both reject the shape itself.

vectors.name: accounts entry that is not an object is rejected
vectors.description: As for persons: the shape is checked before any field of it is read.

vectors.name: conversions entry that is not an object is rejected
vectors.description: As for persons and accounts: the shape is checked before any field of it is read.

vectors.name: account without an ownerId is rejected
vectors.description: ownerId is required in the same way id is. Falling through to the unknown-owner check produced a message naming a nonexistent owner, and the two engines rendered the absent value differently.

vectors.name: conversion without an ownerId is rejected
vectors.description: ownerId is required in the same way id is, for the same reason as on an account.

vectors.name: unrecognized contributionPreference is rejected
vectors.description: A stale or camel-cased enum such as "rothFirst" is not one of account_type, pretax_first, or roth_first. Accepting it and silently falling through to the pretax path returns a plausible but wrong allocation, so it is rejected.

vectors.name: unrecognized employerContributionTaxTreatment is rejected
vectors.description: As for contributionPreference: "PRETAX" is not one of pretax or roth, and silently accepting it returns a number rather than an error.

vectors.name: rate outside 0 through 1 is rejected
vectors.description: employerNonelectiveRate is a fraction of compensation, so 1.5 is not a rate. Pinned here because the two engines worded the same rejection differently.

vectors.name: existing contributions above the account ceiling name the amounts
vectors.description: 2026 IRC 219(b)(5)(A) caps a traditional IRA at 7500 for a taxpayer under 50 (Notice 2025-67), so a supplied 20000 exceeds it by 12500. The diagnostic states both figures; the message is asserted because the two engines carried different wording for the same finding.

expect.accounts.0.diagnostics.0.message: The annual amount $20,000 exceeds the calculated account ceiling of $7,500. Shared-limit records should also be reviewed for excess contributions across accounts.

vectors.name: taxYear that is not an integer is rejected
vectors.description: A string year is not a year. Coercing it silently reported an unsupported-year error naming a year the caller never supplied.

vectors.name: missing filingStatus is rejected rather than defaulted
vectors.description: Filing status selects every phase-out band and the IRC 223(b)(5) spousal rules, so defaulting an absent one to single silently changes the answer.

vectors.name: filingStatus that is not a string is rejected
vectors.description: As above; the value is reported by shape rather than by an engine-specific stringification of it.

vectors.name: accounts that is not an array is rejected
vectors.description: accounts is a list; a scalar in its place is a caller defect, not an empty portfolio.

vectors.name: conversions that is not an array is rejected
vectors.description: As for accounts.

vectors.name: account type that is not a string is rejected
vectors.description: Reported by shape, because interpolating a non-string into the unsupported-type message produced "undefined" in one engine and an empty string in the other.

vectors.name: person id that is not a string is rejected
vectors.description: Identifiers are strings. Coercing 5 to "5" makes the scenario depend on a coercion rule rather than on the input.

vectors.name: structured input field that is not an object is rejected
vectors.description: planRules, existingContributions, compensation, magi, priorYearFicaWagesByEmployer, hsa, hsaCoverage, special403bCatchUp, and section457SpecialCatchUp are objects; a scalar in their place was silently ignored, so every rule they carry vanished without a word.

vectors.name: unrecognized simpleEmployerContributionMethod is rejected
vectors.description: The same defect shape as contributionPreference: neither engine validated it, so an unrecognized method silently fell through to the default employer formula.

vectors.name: 1989 fractional plan-term capacity keeps its fraction in the message
vectors.description: 1989 IRC 415(c)(1)(B) allowed 25 percent of compensation, so 25 percent of 100018 is 25004.50, less the 1989 IRC 402(g) elective-deferral limit of 7627, leaving 17377.50 of capacity that depends on unstated plan terms. The message must print 17,377.5, not a rounded 17,378; PHP rendered money to two decimals where the TypeScript default carries three.

expect.accounts.0.diagnostics.0.message: $17,377.5 of potential annual-additions capacity requires an employer contribution formula or permission for voluntary after-tax contributions.

vectors.name: flag field that is not a boolean is rejected
vectors.description: The string "0" is truthy in JavaScript and falsy in PHP, so coercing it made a 1980 traditional IRA ineligible in one engine and determinate in the other from the same input. Flag fields must be actual booleans; an empty array is the same trap.

vectors.name: 2026 unmarried qualified HSA funding distribution reduces the limit under IRC 223(b)(4)(C)
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces "the limitation which would (but for this paragraph) apply under this subsection" by the sum of its subparagraphs, of which "(C) the aggregate amount contributed to health savings accounts of such individual for such taxable year under section 408(d)(9)". Twelve self-only months give 12 x (4400/12) = 4400 under IRC 223(b)(2)(A) with the 2026 amount from Rev. Proc. 2025-19; the $1,500 rolled over from an IRA under IRC 408(d)(9) reduces it to 4400 - 1500 = 2900.

vectors.name: 2026 qualified HSA funding distribution reaches the IRC 223(b)(3) additional contribution amount
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces the limitation applying "under this subsection", which for an individual who attained 55 before the close of the year is the IRC 223(b)(1) limitation as increased by IRC 223(b)(3). Twelve self-only months in 2026 give 4400 and the IRC 223(b)(3)(B) table gives 1000 for 2009 and thereafter, so subsection (b) allows 5400; a $5,000 IRC 408(d)(9) contribution reduces it to 400. The subsection is reduced once as a whole, so paragraph (1) absorbs 4400 and only the 600 it could not absorb reaches the 1000, leaving 400. hsa.additionalContributionAmount reports the unreduced statutory 1000.

vectors.name: 2026 IRC 223(b)(4) reduces by the sum of subparagraphs (A) and (C) but not below zero
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces the limitation "(but not below zero) by the sum of" its subparagraphs, so 1200 paid to Archer MSAs and 3400 contributed under IRC 408(d)(9) reduce the 2026 twelve-month self-only limitation of 4400 by 4600 and leave 0 rather than -200. The fall is attributed in subparagraph order: (A) takes the first 1200 in full, leaving 3200, and (C) can only reach that 3200 of the remaining ceiling even though 3400 was contributed.

vectors.name: 2026 married qualified HSA funding distribution is taken after the IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) division
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b)(4) flush text says "Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any individual to whom paragraph (5) applies" and names subparagraph (A) alone, so subparagraph (C) survives for a married individual; and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) reduces the family limitation only "by the aggregate amount paid to Archer MSAs of such spouses", so nothing routes (C) through paragraph (5). It is an amount of "such individual", so it reduces that spouse's own subsection (b) limitation after the division. The 2026 family limitation of 8750 divides equally to 4375 each; the taxpayer's $2,000 IRC 408(d)(9) contribution leaves the taxpayer 2375 and the spouse untouched at 4375. Taken before the division like the Archer reduction it would have given (8750 - 2000) / 2 = 3375 to each and charged the spouse for the taxpayer's rollover.

vectors.name: 2026 matched Archer MSA contribution of the same amount is taken before the division instead
vectors.description: The same couple and the same $2,000, paid to Archer MSAs instead of contributed under IRC 408(d)(9), goes through IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) and reduces the single family limitation before (ii) divides it: 8750 - 2000 = 6750 divided equally is 3375 each. Pairing this with the IRC 408(d)(9) vector isolates the ordering rather than the amount — 2375/4375 under subparagraph (C) against 3375/3375 under IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) — which is what the flush text naming only subparagraph (A) produces.

vectors.name: 2026 married qualified HSA funding distribution reaches that spouse's IRC 223(b)(3) amount
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B) reduces and divides the paragraph (1) limitation "without regard to any additional contribution amount under paragraph (3)", so the Archer reduction can never reach a married individual's age-55 amount. Subparagraph (C) is not part of paragraph (5): it reduces the limitation applying to the individual "under this subsection", which after the division is that spouse's 4375 share plus their own 1000, so it does reach it. A $5,000 IRC 408(d)(9) contribution by a taxpayer aged 55 or over takes the 4375 to 0 and the remaining 625 off the 1000, leaving 375; the spouse keeps 4375 + 1000 = 5375.

vectors.name: 2026 qualified HSA funding distribution follows the IRC 223(b)(8) last-month rule on both sides
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(8)(A) applies "for purposes of computing the limitation under paragraph (1)" and IRC 223(b)(4) reduces "the limitation which would (but for this paragraph) apply under this subsection", so the reduction follows the last-month rule. December-only self-only coverage with the election gives 4400, less the $200 contributed under IRC 408(d)(9) is 4200. The counterfactual month-by-month limitation is 4400/12 = 366.67, and the same 200 reduces it to 166.67, so the amount that "could not have been made but for" IRC 223(b)(8)(A) under IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i)(I) is 4200 - 166.67 = 4033.33. Measuring it against the unreduced 366.67 counterfactual would understate it by the 200 that never applied. hsa.contributionLimitWithoutLastMonthRule reports the unreduced 366.67.

vectors.name: 2026 family-limit shares that do not exhaust the limitation are not a division
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) says the limitation "shall be divided equally between them unless they agree on a different division". Shares of 0.3 and 0.3 total 0.6 and divide nothing: they allocate 2625 and 2625 out of the 2026 family limitation of 8750 and leave 3500 belonging to neither spouse. That is the same defect as shares totalling more than 1, which HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_SHARES_EXCEED_ONE already reports at ERROR severity, so it is reported the same way and the result is indeterminate rather than a determinate 2625 that silently forfeits the difference.

vectors.name: 2026 family-limit shares totalling exactly one may still give a spouse nothing
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) constrains the division, not either share within it, so an agreement of 1 and 0 divides the whole 2026 family limitation of 8750 to one spouse and leaves the other 0. The shares total exactly 1, so the division is complete and the result stays determinate: the guard is on the sum, not on any share being positive.

vectors.name: 2026 sole HSA-owning spouse may agree a share below one without forfeiting anything
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides the limitation between the spouses, and the shares that can be supplied cover only spouses who own a health savings account. Where one spouse owns none, a share of 0.6 on the other is a complete division whose remaining 0.4 the first spouse has no account to use, not an under-allocation, so no shares-below-one error applies: 0.6 x 8750 = 5250. Pinning the first diagnostic as the general disclaimer proves neither HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_SHARES_BELOW_ONE nor the equal-division default fired.

vectors.name: 2026 incomplete family-limit shares report only the missing-share error
vectors.description: When one spouse supplies a share of 0.6 and the other supplies none, the division is not incomplete in amount but unstated, which HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_SHARE_REQUIRED_FOR_BOTH_SPOUSES already reports; treating the missing share as 0 and additionally reporting a total below 1 would name the same defect twice. Pinning both diagnostic positions proves no shares-below-one error is inserted between them.

vectors.name: 2026 flexible spending arrangement parameters are published in the result
vectors.description: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 sets the 2026 IRC 125(i) dollar limitation on health FSA salary reduction contributions at 3400 and states that where the cafeteria plan permits a carryover the maximum carryover amount is 680, which is 20 percent of 3400 under Notice 2020-33. Pub. L. 119-21 section 70404 struck "$5,000 ($2,500" from IRC 129(a)(2)(A) and inserted "$7,500 ($3,750" for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, so the 2026 dependent care exclusion is 7500 and 3750 on a married separate return. The scenario result carries these alongside hsaParameters whether or not the scenario holds any flexible spending arrangement.

vectors.name: 2012 health FSA exists with no statutory ceiling rather than not existing
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) reaches plan years beginning after December 31, 2012, so 2012 has no statutory salary-reduction ceiling. The arrangement existed, though, so the row records the state rather than being absent: an absent row means the program did not exist, which is a different fact and produces a different result.

vectors.name: 1986 has an IRC 129 row with no dollar ceiling; 1981 has no row at all
vectors.description: Pub. L. 97-34 section 124 added IRC 129 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1981, and Pub. L. 99-514 section 1163(a) added its dollar limitation for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986. 1986 therefore sits in the middle state: the exclusion existed with no statutory ceiling, which the table records rather than omits. The unavailable years are the ones with no row, which is what makes the table minimum the statement of when IRC 129 began.

vectors.name: 2026 health FSA election at the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 sets the 2026 dollar limitation under IRC 125(i) on voluntary employee salary reductions for contributions to health flexible spending arrangements at 3400, so an employee electing the maximum elects 3400. IRC 125(a) keeps the salary reduction out of gross income, so the whole 3400 comes out of Form W-2 box 1 and out of social security and medicare wages under IRC 3121(a)(5)(G) and none of it appears in federalAgiReduction, which reports above-the-line deductions.

vectors.name: 2013 is the first year IRC 125(i) limits a health FSA election
vectors.description: IRC 125(i)(1) fixes the limit at 2500 and IRC 125(i)(2) begins indexing only for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2013, so 2013 carries the raw statutory amount. No annual revenue procedure states it: Rev. Proc. 2012-41's list of 2013 adjusted items has no Cafeteria Plans entry, and Notice 2012-40 is the operative authority. Paired with the 2012 vector, this pins the effective date rather than the figure alone.

vectors.name: 2012 health FSA has no statutory salary-reduction ceiling
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) was added by Pub. L. 111-148 section 9005 and Notice 2012-40 section II records that before its effective date plan sponsors imposed their own limits but there was no statutory limit. Notice 2012-40 section III reads the effective date as reaching plan years beginning after December 31, 2012. A health FSA therefore existed in 2012 and could receive salary reductions; what did not exist is a ceiling. The result is indeterminate with a null statutory maximum rather than unavailable with a zero, which is what the account type not existing would produce, and rather than a 2500 borrowed from the following year.

vectors.name: 2026 health FSA carryover is capped by the 2025 cap and the excess is forfeited
vectors.description: Notice 2020-33 section III.A sets the carryover at 20 percent of the IRC 125(i) limit for the plan year the amounts are carried FROM, and Rev. Proc. 2024-40 section 3.16 states 660 for a plan year beginning in 2025, which is 20 percent of that year's 3300 limit. Notice 2013-71 section III makes the carried amount the lesser of the unused amount and the cap, and forfeits the rest: 900 unused gives 660 carried and 240 forfeited. The receiving year's cap of 680 is a different figure and does not govern this carryover, which is the error a receiving-year reading would make.

vectors.name: 2026 health FSA carryover sits on top of the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section III holds that in addition to the carried-over amount the plan may permit the individual to elect up to the maximum allowed salary reduction, so the carryover "does not count against or otherwise affect" the IRC 125(i) limit. A 400 carryover out of the 2025 plan year, below that year's 660 cap so nothing is forfeited, therefore leaves the 2026 ceiling at the full 3400 from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15, and 3800 is available to pay claims incurred in 2026. Implementing the carryover as a reduction would give 3000 here, which is why this needs its own vector.

vectors.name: a health FSA grace period precludes a carryover
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section IV holds that a plan providing for a carryover may not also provide a grace period, and conversely a plan that offers the Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.125-1(e) grace period carries nothing over. Nothing is carried in, and no forfeiture figure is produced because how much of the prior year's balance survives depends on expenses incurred during the two-month-and-15-day grace period, which is not a tax parameter. Paired with the carryover vector on the same 900 unused amount, this shows the plan option and not the amount is what decides.

vectors.name: a health FSA offering neither carryover nor grace period forfeits the whole unused amount
vectors.description: Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.125-5(c) requires unused benefits or contributions remaining at the end of the plan year to be forfeited, which Notice 2013-71 calls the use-or-lose rule. A plan that offers no carryover forfeits all 900, not the 240 excess above the 660 cap that a carryover plan would forfeit. The forfeiture is reported rather than silently dropped.

vectors.name: a health FSA carryover and grace period asserted together are refused
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section IV: a section 125 cafeteria plan that incorporates a carryover provision may not also provide for a grace period in the plan year to which unused amounts may be carried over. Asserting both describes a plan that cannot exist, so a determinate carryover figure computed from either fact would assert something the guidance forbids. The result is indeterminate with no statutory maximum and no carryover cap, following the treatment of shares that do not divide the IRC 223(b)(5) family limitation.

vectors.name: nothing may be carried into 2013, the first year the carryover existed
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section IV permits a plan to adopt the carryover for a plan year beginning in 2013, so 2013 is the first plan year amounts may be carried FROM and 2014 the first year they may land in. There is consequently no 2012 cap, and a 2013 scenario asserting a carryover of a prior-year unused amount cannot be answered: the cap that governs belongs to the source year. Reporting zero carried would be indistinguishable from a plan that forfeited, so the result is indeterminate.

vectors.name: a 2021 health FSA carryover out of 2020 discloses that CAA 2021 section 214 relief is not modelled
vectors.description: Rev. Proc. 2019-44 section 3.17 sets the 2020 IRC 125(i) limit at 2750 and Notice 2020-33 section III.A states 550 as the maximum unused amount from a plan year starting in 2020, being 20 percent of 2750. Section 214 of Pub. L. 116-260, implemented by Notice 2021-15 section III.A, separately permitted a plan to carry over ALL unused amounts from a plan year ending in 2020 to the plan year ending in 2021. Adopting that was entirely a plan option, so the ordinary cap is applied and the divergence is disclosed rather than left silent: 900 unused gives 550 carried under the ordinary cap and would give 900 under section 214 relief.

vectors.name: a prior-year unused amount without a stated plan option asks for the fact
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 makes the carryover and the grace period plan options that a plan may adopt, may adopt one of, or may adopt neither, and they are mutually exclusive. An unused amount alone therefore does not determine what happens to it. Assuming a carryover would report 660 carried and assuming forfeiture would report 900 forfeited, so the engine reports neither, asks for the fact, and marks the result determinate with assumptions.

vectors.name: a health FSA election above the IRC 125(i) limit is reported, not truncated
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) makes a health FSA a qualified benefit only if the plan provides that an employee may not elect salary reduction contributions above the limit, and Notice 2012-40 section III holds that a plan failing to comply is not a section 125 cafeteria plan at all, so the value of the taxable benefits the employee could have elected is includible regardless of the benefit elected. A 4000 election for 2026 against the 3400 limit from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 is therefore an error carrying a plan-qualification consequence, and truncating it to 3400 would report a smaller consequence than the statute produces. The 600 excess is reported and nothing further is allocated. Notice 2012-40 section III costs the plan its IRC 125 status entirely rather than only as to the excess, so the IRC 125(a) exclusion fails for the whole 4000: the election stays in contributionComponents as a fact, and no wage exclusion is reported for it.

vectors.name: an account type that did not exist for the tax year reports no exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 223 was added by the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 section 1201 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2003, so there is no health savings account for 2003. A cafeteria-plan contribution supplied against one is still recorded, because the scenario said it happened, but it cannot carry the IRC 106(d) exclusion of an account type that did not exist: no reduction of Form W-2 box 1 wages and none of social security and medicare wages is reported.

vectors.name: a pre-2013 health FSA still excludes its salary reduction under IRC 125(a)
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) was added by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act section 9005 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2012, so 2012 has no statutory salary reduction ceiling to report and the account is indeterminate. The arrangement existed, though, and IRC 125(a) excluded its salary reduction from gross income exactly as it does now. An indeterminate limit is not a reason to withhold the exclusion: the 3000 elected is outside Form W-2 box 1 and outside social security and medicare wages. This is the deliberate contrast with an unavailable account type and with an IRC 125(i) qualification failure, where the exclusion genuinely does not apply.

vectors.name: a pre-2013 health FSA with a supplied plan maximum reports that maximum
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) reaches plan years beginning after December 31, 2012, so 2012 has no statutory salary-reduction ceiling. The arrangement existed and the ceiling was whatever the plan document imposed. Where the caller supplies that document, the maximum is knowable and is reported: the statutory maximum stays null because no statute set one, while the maximum the inputs support is the plan's own 2000. Refusing to answer here would discard a fact the caller gave, and a diagnostic records that the figure rests on the plan term alone.

vectors.name: two unrelated employers each carry a full health FSA limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: an employee employed by two or more employers that are not members of the same controlled group may elect up to the indexed limit under each employer's health FSA. For 2026 that is 3400 under each of two unrelated employers and 6800 in total, which is the answer a single per-person limit would get wrong.

vectors.name: two health FSAs of one employer share a single IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: all employers treated as a single employer under IRC 414(b), (c) or (m) are treated as one for the limit, and an employee participating in multiple cafeteria plans of that group is limited to the indexed amount in total under IRC 125(g)(4). Two arrangements carrying the same employerId therefore draw on one 3400 pool for 2026, not two, so the first exhausts it and the second has nothing left. Paired with the two-unrelated-employers vector, this pins that employerId is what separates the limits.

vectors.name: spouses filing jointly each carry a full health FSA limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: the limit applies on an employee-by-employee basis, so if each of two spouses is eligible to elect salary reduction contributions each may elect up to the indexed amount, even in the same health FSA sponsored by the same employer. For 2026 that is 3400 each and 6800 in total. This is the deliberate contrast with IRC 129(a)(2)(A), which is a per-return household amount.

vectors.name: non-elective employer flex credits stay outside the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: the limit applies only to salary reduction contributions and not to employer non-elective contributions, sometimes called flex credits, and its worked example is an employer contributing a 500 flex credit to each employee's health FSA for the plan year, after which each employee may still elect the full indexed amount. For 2026 the employee therefore still elects 3400 alongside a 500 non-elective credit.

vectors.name: flex credits electable as cash consume the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: if an employer provides flex credits that employees may elect to receive as cash or as a taxable benefit, those flex credits are treated as salary reduction contributions for purposes of IRC 125(i). A 500 cashable credit against the 3400 limit from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 therefore leaves 2900 of election room. Paired with the non-elective vector at the same 500, this pins that the cash election and not the credit is what matters.

vectors.name: flex credits without a stated cash election ask for the fact
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 makes the answer turn entirely on whether the employee could have elected the credit as cash or another taxable benefit, and that is a plan-design fact this engine cannot read. The ordinary case under Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.125-5(b) is a non-elective credit, so the full 3400 is reported, but the assumption is stated rather than silent and the status records it.

vectors.name: a lower plan-document health FSA limit binds
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section III records that a plan may specify a lower amount than the statutory maximum, and Notice 2012-40 section II notes that before IRC 125(i) plan sponsors imposed their own limits. A plan capping elections at 2000 for 2026 therefore binds below the 3400 statutory ceiling. The two are reported separately rather than merged: statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution is what IRC 125(i) sets, and maximumAnnualContributionBasedOnInputs is what the supplied plan document allows within it. Reporting 2000 as the statutory maximum would attribute the plan sponsor's own term to the statute.

vectors.name: a lower plan-document limit caps its own arrangement, not the employer group
vectors.description: IRC 125(g)(4) treats employers under IRC 414(b), (c) or (m) as one employer, which Notice 2012-40 applies to aggregate elections across their cafeteria plans against the one statutory ceiling. It aggregates to the statutory amount; it does not turn one plan's own lower term into an employer-wide ceiling. A plan document capping elections at 2000 binds elections under that plan and gives it no power over a different plan of the same group, so for 2026 the first arrangement reaches 2000, the second reaches the 1400 left of the shared 3400, and the group total is 3400 rather than 2000.

vectors.name: exceeding a plan-document limit is not the IRC 125(i) qualification failure
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III holds that a cafeteria plan permitting an election above the IRC 125(i) limit is not an IRC 125 cafeteria plan at all, which is why an election above the statutory ceiling reports no IRC 125(a) exclusion. That holding addresses the statutory limit. An election of 3000 against a plan document allowing 2000 stays within the 3400 IRC 125(i) ceiling for 2026, so it is a plan-operation question rather than a statutory qualification failure: it is reported, but the exclusion is not withdrawn, and the 3000 remains outside Form W-2 box 1 and outside social security and medicare wages.

vectors.name: a non-calendar cafeteria plan year makes the IRC 125(i) figure indeterminate
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III holds that "taxable year" in IRC 125(i) refers to the plan year of the cafeteria plan, so the limit runs on a plan-year basis and a short plan year is prorated by its months, while every annual revenue procedure publishes the figure for taxable years beginning in a calendar year and this package is keyed by tax year. The two agree exactly for a calendar-year plan. For any other plan year the governing figure depends on the plan year start date, which is not an input, so the result is indeterminate rather than the calendar-year figure assumed.

vectors.name: a bare FSA account type is rejected as ambiguous
vectors.description: Input-contract assertion rather than a computed amount. "FSA" names an IRC 125(i) health flexible spending arrangement and an IRC 129 dependent care assistance program equally well, and the two carry different limits, different authorities, and different household aggregation - IRC 125(i) is per employee per employer while IRC 129(a)(2)(A) is per return. Aliasing the bare string would silently pick one of them, so it is rejected and the message names both spellings.

vectors.name: an unrecognised health FSA purpose is rejected
vectors.description: Input-contract assertion rather than a computed amount. Rev. Rul. 2004-45 classifies a health FSA as general-purpose, limited-purpose, or post-deductible, and the three lead to different IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) answers. A fourth spelling is not a fourth classification, so it is rejected rather than treated as unstated, which would silently downgrade a stated fact into the diagnose-and-ask path.

vectors.name: 2025 dependent care assistance exclusion on a single return
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) sets the amount excludable for dependent care services provided during a taxable year at 5000, and the amount is not inflation adjusted, so no revenue procedure states it and 2025 carries the same figure the Tax Reform Act of 1986 put there. IRC 129(a)(1) excludes it from gross income, so it comes out of Form W-2 box 1 and out of social security and medicare wages under IRC 3121(a)(18) and contributes nothing to federalAgiReduction. The employee's 60000 of earned income does not bind under IRC 129(b)(1)(A).

vectors.name: 2025 dependent care exclusion is halved on a married separate return
vectors.description: The IRC 129(a)(2)(A) parenthetical sets the amount at 2500 in the case of a separate return by a married individual. Married separate spouses file separate returns, so each carries their own 2500 rather than dividing one 5000, which is why the amount is halved rather than shared. IRC 129(b)(1)(B) needs both spouses' earned income; 60000 and 55000 leave the statutory amount binding. IRC 129(a)(2)(C) takes marital status from IRC 21(e)(3) and (4) rather than from the filing status alone, and the IRC 21(e)(4) facts are not derivable from anything supplied, so the halved amount is applied and the undetermined status is reported rather than assumed away.

vectors.name: an IRC 21(e)(4) considered-unmarried separate return takes the undivided amount
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(C) determines marital status under IRC 21(e)(3) and (4). IRC 21(e)(4) treats a married individual filing separately as not married when they maintained a household that was a qualifying individual's principal place of abode for more than half the taxable year, furnished over half the cost of maintaining it, and their spouse was not a member of it during the last six months. Such a taxpayer is not married for IRC 129, so for 2026 they take the undivided 7500 rather than the halved 3750, and the IRC 129(b)(1)(A) limitation is their own 90000 earned income rather than the IRC 129(b)(1)(B) lesser of the two spouses' 3000. Both halves of the rule move together: applying one without the other reproduces neither the married nor the unmarried treatment.

vectors.name: a separate return that states it is still married keeps the halved amount
vectors.description: The contrast with the vector above. Stating treatedAsUnmarriedUnderSection21e4 as false is the IRC 21(e)(4) determination made and answered in the negative, so the halved 3750 and the IRC 129(b)(1)(B) lesser-of rule apply exactly as they do without the fact -- but the result is determinate rather than carrying the undetermined-status warning, because the caller has answered the question.

vectors.name: 2021 only, the ARPA dependent care exclusion is 10500
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(D), added by the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, Pub. L. 117-2 section 9632(a), applies subparagraph (A) for a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2022 by substituting "$10,500 (half such dollar amount" for "$5,000 ($2,500". The statute writes the separate-return amount as half rather than as a number, and half of 10500 is 5250. Enacted in March 2021, so Rev. Proc. 2020-45 could not carry it; the authority is the act.

vectors.name: 2022 reverts to the pre-ARPA dependent care exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(D) reaches only a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2022, so the substitution lapses and subparagraph (A) applies unmodified from 2022: 5000, or 2500 on a married separate return. A 2021-only vector passes even if the reversion is missing entirely, which is why the pair is needed rather than the single year.

vectors.name: 2026 dependent care exclusion rises to 7500 under Pub. L. 119-21
vectors.description: Pub.
