L. 119-21 section 70404(a) amends IRC 129(a)(2)(A) by striking "$5,000 ($2,500" and inserting "$7,500 ($3,750", and section 70404(b) applies the amendment to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. It is a fixed-dollar substitution that adds no indexing mechanism. Paired with the 2025 vector this pins the effective date; the 2024 edition of the Code still prints the old figures, so a year block generated from the Code text alone would be wrong here.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) earned income limitation binds below the statutory amount
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(1)(B) caps the amount excluded at the lesser of the employee's and the spouse's earned income for the taxable year. A spouse with 3000 of earned income against the employee's 90000 therefore caps the exclusion at 3000, well below the 7500 that IRC 129(a)(2)(A) allows for 2026. Both figures are caller-supplied, which is what keeps this inside a package that does not derive income. The two ceilings are reported separately: statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution is the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount and maximumAnnualContributionBasedOnInputs is what the supplied earned income allows within it.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) limitation is asked for when the earned income facts are absent
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(1)(B) caps the exclusion at the lesser of the employee's and the spouse's earned income, and on a joint return both are needed. Only the employee's is supplied here. The ceiling is mandatory rather than an optional refinement, so reporting the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount as what the inputs support would assume the missing spouse's earned income is at least 7500 -- an assumption the statute never permits. The result fails closed: the statutory amount is still reported, the amount the inputs support is null, and the diagnostic names the missing fact.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(2) deemed earned income schedule is disclosed as unmodelled
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(2) applies IRC 21(d)(2) to deem earned income for a spouse who is a student or incapable of caring for himself. The IRC 21(d)(2) monthly schedule is a figure this package does not encode, because no primary source for it is committed to the evidence corpus and an unattested amount is never encoded. The supplied spouse figure of 500 is therefore used exactly as stated - as the deemed amount - and the divergence is disclosed rather than silently filled in. Both earned income figures are supplied, so the result stays determinate with assumptions rather than failing closed; what is disclosed is that the supplied 500 is used exactly as stated rather than derived from the IRC 21(d)(2) schedule.

vectors.name: spouses filing jointly share one IRC 129 household exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) limits the amount which may be excluded for dependent care services provided during a taxable year, and IRC 129(a)(2)(C) determines marital status under IRC 21(e)(3) and (4); it is a per-return figure, not a per-person one. Two spouses electing 5000 each for 2026 against the 7500 household amount therefore exclude 7500 in total, not 15000, and IRC 129(a)(2)(B) includes the remaining 2500 in gross income for the taxable year the services were provided. This is the deliberate contrast with IRC 125(i), which is per employee and gives each spouse a full limit.

vectors.name: married separate spouses do not share one IRC 129 exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) is per return and married separate spouses file two returns, so each carries their own halved 3750 amount for 2026 rather than dividing a single 7500. Two 3750 elections are therefore both wholly excludable and nothing is includible, which pooling them would get wrong by including 3750. Paired with the joint vector on the same two elections, this pins that filing status and not marriage decides the pooling.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) ceiling is a return-level figure across two dependent care FSAs
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(1) caps "the amount excluded from the income of an employee under subsection (a) for any taxable year", which is that year's aggregate rather than a per-plan figure, and Form 2441 Part III computes one excluded-benefits amount for the return as the smallest of the benefits received, the employee's earned income, the spouse's earned income, and the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount. A spouse earning 3000 therefore caps the whole return at 3000, not at 3000 for each dependent care FSA it holds: of the 10000 elected across two arrangements, 3000 is excluded and IRC 129(a)(2)(B) includes the remaining 7000 in gross income. Applied per account the same facts would exclude 6000.

vectors.name: a dependent care plan document below the IRC 129 amount binds this arrangement
vectors.description: Form 2441's dependent care benefit computation takes the maximum permitted under the employer's plan into account when it is below the Code amount. A plan allowing 4000 for 2026 therefore binds below the 7500 IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount, and the statutory figure is still reported separately so the source of the constraint is visible rather than merged into one number.

vectors.name: a dependent care plan document caps its own arrangement, not the household amount
vectors.description: The IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount is the return's and a plan document is one plan's own term, so the two constrain different things. For 2026 an arrangement allowing 2000 reaches 2000, and a second arrangement with no such term still reaches the remaining 5500 of the 7500 household amount. A plan document that lowered the household figure would forfeit 5500 of capacity the Code allows.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) ceiling does not pool across married separate returns
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) gives a married individual filing separately half the amount, and the two spouses file two returns rather than one, so each draws on its own 3750 for 2026. The IRC 129(b)(1) ceiling follows the same scope: it caps the exclusion on each return, so a lesser earned income of 3000 binds each return at 3000 rather than binding 3000 across both. Each spouse electing 3500 therefore excludes 3000 and includes 500, and the pair excludes 6000 in total. This is the deliberate contrast with the joint-return vector above, where one ceiling covers both arrangements.

vectors.name: 1986 dependent care has no statutory ceiling, so the earned income limitation is the ceiling
vectors.description: Pub. L. 99-514 section 1163(a) added the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) dollar limitation for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986, so 1986 has none. IRC 129 existed and excluded the assistance, and IRC 129(b)(1) still capped it at the employee's earned income. With 40000 of earned income supplied that is the only ceiling there was, and it is a real answer: the statutory maximum is null while the maximum the inputs support is 40000. Reporting nothing here would discard a fact the caller gave.

vectors.name: 1986 dependent care with no ceiling from any source stays indeterminate
vectors.description: The contrast with the vector above. Without a statutory ceiling, and with neither the IRC 129(b)(1) earned income facts nor a plan maximum supplied, there is no ceiling from any source and no maximum is reported. The absence of a statutory figure is not by itself a reason to refuse; the absence of every figure is.

vectors.name: 1981 predates IRC 129 entirely
vectors.description: The effective-date note to IRC 129 makes the section applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1981, under section 124(f) of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, Pub. L. 97-34. For 1981 there was no dependent care assistance exclusion at all, which is a different fact from the 1982 through 1986 years where the exclusion existed without a ceiling. The two therefore report differently: unavailable with a zero here, indeterminate with a null there.

vectors.name: a health FSA and a dependent care FSA carry independent limits
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) limits salary reduction contributions to a health flexible spending arrangement and Notice 2012-40 section III states expressly that it does not limit employee salary reduction contributions to an FSA for dependent care assistance, which IRC 129(a)(2)(A) governs separately. For 2026 an employee may therefore elect 3400 under Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 and 7500 under IRC 129(a)(2)(A) as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 section 70404, and the two figures never draw on one another.

vectors.name: a general-purpose health FSA is diagnosed against an HSA without changing the IRC 223 figures
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 Situation 1 holds that an individual covered by an HDHP and by a health FSA paying or reimbursing section 213(d) medical expenses before the IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) minimum annual deductible is satisfied is not an eligible individual, because IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) requires that an eligible individual not be covered by a plan that is not an HDHP and that provides coverage for a benefit the HDHP covers. The conflict is reported and not enforced: eligible-individual status is a caller-supplied fact everywhere in this engine and no rule overrides one, so the caller who has already accounted for it still gets the answer their months imply. Rev. Proc. 2025-19 sets the 2026 IRC 223(b)(2)(A) self-only limitation at 4400, and that figure and the amount the inputs support must both survive untouched - asserting them is the whole point, since a rule that zeroed or reduced the limit would still pass a vector that only checked the diagnostic.

vectors.name: a limited-purpose health FSA raises no IRC 223 conflict
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 Situation 2 holds that where the medical expenses paid or reimbursed include only vision and dental benefits, which are permitted coverage, and preventive care, the individual is an eligible individual. No conflict diagnostic is emitted and the account stays determinate, which is what separates this from the general-purpose case on otherwise identical inputs.

vectors.name: a post-deductible health FSA raises no IRC 223 conflict
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 Situation 4 holds that where the health FSA pays or reimburses medical expenses only after the HDHP's minimum annual deductible has been satisfied, including coinsurance the HDHP does not cover, the individual is an eligible individual. The third of the three Rev. Rul. 2004-45 classifications, encoded because it produces the opposite answer from the first on the same account type.

vectors.name: a health FSA of unstated purpose makes the IRC 223 limitation indeterminate
vectors.description: The three Rev. Rul. 2004-45 classifications give two opposite IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) answers, and which applies is a plan-design fact this engine cannot read. Unlike the general-purpose case, where the conflict is known and the caller's own figures are returned, here nothing about IRC 223 is known, so a confident 4400 would be the defect rather than the diagnostic. The limitation is refused and the purpose is asked for. The health FSA's own disqualifiesHsaEligibility is null for the same reason.

vectors.name: a spouse's general-purpose health FSA disqualifies the other spouse's HSA
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 states expressly, after the Situation 1 holding, that the result is the same if the individual is covered by a health FSA sponsored by the employer of the individual's spouse, because such an arrangement can reimburse this individual's own section 213(d) medical expenses. The conflict is household-level, not per-person. The diagnostic lands on the HSA owner's account even though the arrangement belongs to the other spouse, and the IRC 223(b) figures are unchanged for the same reason they are in the individual case. The spouse's empty persons[].hsaCoverage records that they held no HDHP coverage, which is what IRC 223(b)(5)(A) needs to know.

vectors.name: a general-purpose health FSA carryover disqualifies the whole receiving plan year
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 makes the carried-over amount available to pay medical expenses incurred during the entire plan year to which it is carried. Carried-over general-purpose funds are therefore general-purpose coverage for that whole year, not just until they are spent, so the Rev. Rul. 2004-45 disqualification reaches the receiving year rather than a part of it. Rev. Proc. 2024-40 section 3.16 caps the carryover out of 2025 at 660, and the diagnostic says so; the IRC 223 figures are unchanged as in every other branch of this interaction.

vectors.name: a general-purpose health FSA grace period extends the IRC 223 disqualification
vectors.description: Notice 2005-86 holds that an individual participating in a health FSA who is covered by the grace period is generally not eligible to contribute to an HSA until the first day of the first month following the end of that grace period, even where the participant's health FSA has no unused benefits at the end of the prior plan year. The grace-period months fall in the following plan year, which this year's eligible-month input cannot express, so the extension is reported as information alongside the disqualification rather than folded into the month list.

vectors.name: a dependent care FSA raises no IRC 223 conflict at all
vectors.description: IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) reaches coverage providing a benefit the high deductible health plan covers, and an IRC 129 dependent care assistance program reimburses dependent care expenses rather than section 213(d) medical expenses, so Rev. Rul. 2004-45 has nothing to say about it. A dependent care FSA alongside an HSA is therefore an ordinary determinate scenario, which is worth pinning because the two account types were added together and a purpose check written against the wrong family would fire here.

vectors.name: 2026 defined benefit plan reports the IRC 415(b)(1)(A) annual benefit limit
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 states that effective January 1, 2026 "the limitation on the annual benefit under a defined benefit plan under section 415(b)(1)(A) of the Code is increased from $280,000 to $290,000", so the 2026 annual benefit limit is $290,000; the figure is transcribed from that notice in evidence/retirement-limits and its document is fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt. That limitation caps the benefit the plan may pay and is not a contribution ceiling: sizing a defined-benefit contribution runs through IRC 404, IRC 412 and the ERISA funding rules from the plan formula, participant census, assets and actuarial assumptions, none of which this package models. The account therefore keeps a null statutory maximum, an indeterminate status and DEFINED_BENEFIT_CONTRIBUTION_REQUIRES_ACTUARIAL_VALUATION, and reports the benefit limit beside them. Pinning both halves is the point: the benefit ceiling is knowable from the tax year alone, the contribution is not, and neither answer may be derived from the other.

vectors.name: 2011 cash balance plan reports the transcribed IRC 415(b)(1)(A) annual benefit limit
vectors.description: A cash balance plan is a defined benefit plan that states the benefit as a hypothetical account balance, so IRC 415(b) governs it and IRC 415(c) does not; it takes the same treatment here as a traditional pension. Notice 2010-78 states that effective January 1, 2011 "the limitation on the annual benefit under a defined benefit plan under 415(b)(1)(A) remains unchanged at $195,000". "Remains unchanged" is the notice publishing the figure for 2011, not declining to: an amount the IRS restates for a year is transcribed for that year like any other, and 195000 is recorded for 2011 in evidence/retirement-limits from the document fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt. It is not carried forward from the 195000 recorded for 2010, which SOURCES.md would forbid. The account still keeps a null statutory maximum and an indeterminate status, because IRC 415(b)(1)(A) caps the benefit the plan may pay and says nothing about the contribution needed to fund it; the actuarial-valuation diagnostic is therefore still the first diagnostic on the account, with the benefit-limit report beside it.

vectors.name: 2012 cash balance plan reports the transcribed IRC 415(b)(1)(A) annual benefit limit
vectors.description: A cash balance plan is a defined benefit plan that states the benefit as a hypothetical account balance, so IRC 415(b) governs it and IRC 415(c) does not; it takes the same treatment here as a traditional pension. Notice 2011-90 states that effective January 1, 2012 "the limitation on the annual benefit under a defined benefit plan under 415(b)(1)(A) is increased from $195,000 to $200,000". The figure is transcribed for 2012 in evidence/retirement-limits from the document fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt, and is neither carried forward from the 195000 recorded for 2011 nor interpolated toward the 205000 recorded for 2013, both of which SOURCES.md forbids. The account still keeps a null statutory maximum and an indeterminate status, because IRC 415(b)(1)(A) caps the benefit the plan may pay and says nothing about the contribution needed to fund it; the actuarial-valuation diagnostic is therefore still the first diagnostic on the account, with the benefit-limit report beside it.

vectors.name: 2001 403(b) is indeterminate because the IRC 403(b)(2) exclusion allowance still governs
vectors.description: Before EGTRRA, IRC 403(b)(2) capped the amount excludable from a tax-sheltered annuity at the exclusion allowance, and IRS Publication 571 (2001) chapter 5 computes the maximum amount contributable as the LEAST of that allowance, the IRC 415(c) limit on annual additions and the IRC 402(g) limit on elective deferrals. The allowance is 20 percent of includible compensation for the most recent year of service, multiplied by years of service, reduced by amounts previously excludable; that last term is a lifetime aggregate over the participant service with the employer and no ScenarioInput field supplies it. With the allowance unknown, the least of three cannot be identified, so no universal maximum exists and both the statutory maximum and the input-supported maximum are null rather than the 13500 the other two limits alone would produce (IRC 402(g) 10500 for 2001 plus the IRC 402(g)(7)(A)(i) 15-year catch-up of 3000). SOURCES.md already states this policy for legacy 403(b) exclusion allowances; before this vector the engines contradicted it. The IRC 415(c) pool is still reported without being consumed, and its limit is the lesser of the 35000 dollar amount and the 25 percent of 80000 compensation that IRC 415(c)(1)(B) then imposed, which is 20000. 2001 is the last governed year: EGTRRA (Pub. L. 107-16) section 632(a)(2)(B) struck IRC 403(b)(2), section 632(a)(3)(E) struck the IRC 415(c)(4) elections, and section 632(a)(4) applies both to years beginning after December 31, 2001.

vectors.name: 2002 403(b) is determinable because EGTRRA repealed the exclusion allowance
vectors.description: EGTRRA (Pub. L. 107-16) section 632(a)(2)(A) replaced the words "the exclusion allowance for such taxable year" in IRC 403(b)(1) with "the applicable limit under section 415", section 632(a)(2)(B) struck IRC 403(b)(2) outright, section 632(a)(3)(E) struck IRC 415(c)(4), and section 632(a)(4) applies all of them to years beginning after December 31, 2001. Section 611(d) set the IRC 402(g) applicable dollar amount for taxable years beginning in 2002 at 11000, and IRC 402(g)(7)(A)(i) adds 3000 of 15-year catch-up for an employee with 20 years of service, whose 15000 lifetime cap and 5000-per-year service cap are both unreached, giving an employee-supported maximum of 14000. vectors.name: 1986 403(b) still reports the missing IRC 415(c) limit rather than the exclusion allowance

Both diagnoses reach the same answer of indeterminate and a null maximum, and stating the more specific missing figure is more useful than stating the exclusion allowance on top of it. This pins the ordering: the exclusion-allowance check sits after the IRC 415(c) check, so 1986 keeps the diagnostic it always had and the pre-2002 window observably begins at 1987.

vectors.name: 2001 401(k) is unaffected by the IRC 403(b)(2) exclusion allowance

A 2001 401(k) on the same facts therefore stays answerable: IRC 415(c) is the lesser of the 35000 dollar amount and the 25 percent of 80000 compensation then required by IRC 415(c)(1)(B), which is 20000, and the IRC 402(g) limit for 2001 is 10500, with no age-50 catch-up because IRC 414(v) was added by EGTRRA section 631 only for years beginning after December 31, 2001 and the participant is 41 in any event. vectors.name: a plan sponsor's lower IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount binds below the statutory figure

The statutory maximum stays at the $2,600 the Code and the notice fix, because it reports the legal ceiling rather than the plan's; only the amount supportable on the supplied facts falls to $1,000. vectors.name: a pension-linked emergency savings account needs no birth year
vectors.description: Age matters to an elective-deferral account only through IRC 414(v), which lets a participant who attains age 50 exceed an applicable limit. No catch-up reaches this account: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) forbids any contribution that would push the participant-contribution balance past the ceiling, whatever the participant's age, and IRC 414(v)(3) does not displace that bar. vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's contradictory coverage tiers leave IRC 223(b)(5)(A) applicability unknown, self-only account listed first
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats both spouses as having family coverage for any month in which either of them has it, so an owner with a self-only month cannot be priced without knowing the other spouse's coverage: for 2026 the answer is either the undivided self-only 4400 plus the IRC 223(b)(3) age-55 1000, or a divided family limitation instead. vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's coverage conflict outside the owner's eligible months leaves the owner determinate
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(1) sums twelve separate monthly limitations, and IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats a spouse as having family coverage only for a month in which the other spouse has it, so the applicability of that subsection is a monthly question and not an annual one. The taxpayer here is an eligible individual in December alone, with self-only coverage, so IRC 223(b)(2)(A) gives one twelfth of the 2026 self-only annual amount of 4400, which is 366.67 to the cent. vectors.name: 2026 family sharing survives a spouse's conflict confined to an annual deductible that no longer applies
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives spouses who have family coverage a single family limitation, 8750 for 2026, and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides it equally between them absent an agreed division, giving the taxpayer 4375. Every operand of that calculation is agreed here. The spouse's two health savings accounts both state self-only coverage for the whole year and differ only in the plan's annual deductible. A deductible reaches the limitation in only two ways, and neither is present: IRC 223(b)(2) capped each month at one twelfth of the lesser of the deductible and the dollar amount only for 2004 through 2006, the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303 having removed that cap for later years; and IRC 223(b)(5)(A) takes the lowest annual deductible only where the spouses each have family coverage under different plans, which a self-only plan is not. The spouse's own accounts remain indeterminate under the identical-person-facts contract, but an uncertainty that cannot reach an operand must not be projected onto the result that operand feeds.

vectors.description: The control in the other direction for the 2026 deductible vector above. For 2004 through 2006 IRC 223(b)(2) capped each month's limitation at one twelfth of the lesser of the plan's annual deductible and the statutory dollar amount, and IRC 223(b)(5)(A) takes the lowest annual deductible of the spouses' plans where each has family coverage under a different plan. Both spouses state family coverage here, so the deductible is an operand of the couple's single limitation, and the spouse's two accounts give different family-plan deductibles of 3000 and 4000. The IRC 223(b)(5) household ceiling adds each spouse's undivided self-only months to the divided family limitation, so this spouse's self-only months are worth a different amount under a 2000 deductible than under a 3000 one and the ceiling is not one number. vectors.name: 2026 an age-50 catch-up fills pension-linked emergency savings room the 401(k) host's base pool has no space for
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) bars a contribution only "to the extent such contribution would cause the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions to exceed" the cap, so it gates a balance and is indifferent to how the contribution is characterised. IRC 414(v)(1) lets a participant who attains age 50 before the close of the year (IRC 414(v)(5)(A)) contribute in excess of an applicable limit, and 26 CFR 1.414(v)-1(b)(1)(i) enumerates the limits it relieves — IRC 401(a)(30), 402(h), 403(b), 408, 415(c) and 457(b)(2) — every one a plan- or employee-level limit and none of them account-level. The two compose, so a contribution the host's base limit can no longer accept may still be made within the account's own room. Here the 401(k) recognizes $24,500 of compensation and defers all of it, exhausting the $24,500 IRC 402(g)(1) limit Notice 2025-67 states for 2026 and leaving the emergency savings account no base capacity, while the host's own recognized compensation is spent so it takes no catch-up of its own. The participant attained age 56 in 2026, so the $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) catch-up the same notice states is still available, and the account's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) room of $2,600 less a $0 balance is filled from it: $2,600 is the lesser of the room and the $8,000 remaining. IRC 414(v)(3)(A)(i) provides that a catch-up contribution is not taken into account for IRC 415, so the annual-additions group is not charged for it, and the amount is Roth because IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account "for purposes of this title as a designated Roth account". The reported statutory maximum is the lesser of the host's statutory annual capacity ($24,500 + $8,000) and what the participant has contributed plus the room that remains ($0 + $2,600), so $2,600.

vectors.name: 2026 the same age-50 catch-up fills pension-linked emergency savings room on a 403(b) host

Nothing in IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) or IRC 414(v) turns on which of the two hosts the account sits in, so the same $2,600 of room is filled from the same $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) catch-up. This vector exists because the two hosts reach the allocation through different account types and traits, and a change that fixed only the 401(k) path would leave the 403(b) one reporting a maximum it never allocates.

vectors.name: 2026 a plan sponsor's lower IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount binds the base and the catch-up together
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps the participant-contribution portion of the balance at the lesser of the clause (i) figure and "such lower amount as the plan sponsor may determine" under clause (ii). Because the cap is on the resulting balance rather than on a category of contribution, a $1,000 sponsor amount bounds base deferrals and IRC 414(v) catch-up contributions together: with the host's IRC 402(g)(1) pool exhausted the catch-up may add $1,000 and no more, where a cap applied to the base allocation alone would have let a later catch-up carry the balance past it. The reported statutory maximum stays $2,600 — the clause (i) figure less a $0 balance, bounded by the host's statutory capacity — because a sponsor amount is a plan term rather than encoded law, which is the same line README documents for every other plan-document restriction.

vectors.name: 2026 the pension-linked emergency savings balance and existing contributions are not subtracted twice
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps "the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions", a quantity stated as of the moment before the contribution in question. The supplied balance therefore already contains the $600 deferred earlier in the same year that is still in the account: the $600 is inside the $1,000, not beside it. Room is $2,600 less $1,000 = $1,600, and that is what may still be contributed; subtracting the existing $600 a second time would charge the same dollars twice and would report $1,000. The annual maximum is the $600 already contributed plus that $1,600, so $2,200, and the statutory maximum is the lesser of the host's statutory annual capacity ($24,500 under IRC 402(g)(1) plus the $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) catch-up available at age 56) and what the participant has contributed plus the room that remains ($600 + $1,600), so $2,200 as well. Reporting only the additional amount would leave the statutory maximum free to contradict the annual total, which is why all four figures are asserted.

vectors.name: 2026 a replenished pension-linked emergency savings account may take more in the year than the balance cap
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(7) requires the plan to permit withdrawal from the account at least once a month, and the Department of Labor's PLESA guidance states that a plan may not impose a separate annual contribution limit on the account, precisely because a participant must be able to replenish it after a withdrawal. IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps a balance and not a year's contributions, so the two are different quantities: $600 was contributed this year but only $200 is still attributable to participant contributions, the rest having been withdrawn. Room is $2,600 less $200 = $2,400, the annual total reaches $600 + $2,400 = $3,000, and $3,000 exceeds the $2,600 cap without offending it, because at no point does the balance. A reading of the supplied figure as an opening or prior-year balance could not produce this result without a withdrawal input the package does not have, which is why the field is defined as the balance immediately before the proposed allocation.

vectors.name: 2026 a pension-linked emergency savings account needs a birth year only once a catch-up could reach its room
vectors.description: A birth year is required to size an IRC 414(v) catch-up, but only where the catch-up could change the answer. The companion vector "a pension-linked emergency savings account needs no birth year" holds the case where the host's base capacity covers the whole of the IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) room, so the account is determinate without one. Here the 401(k) has exhausted the $24,500 IRC 402(g)(1) limit, the account's $2,600 of room is untouched, and the participant still has compensation to defer, so whether a catch-up is available — a question only the birth year answers — decides whether the answer is $0 or $2,600. The engine reports BIRTH_YEAR_OR_DATE_REQUIRED_FOR_WORKPLACE_CATCH_UP and returns null rather than guessing, because an overstated ceiling is what exposes a taxpayer to the IRC 4973 excise. The owner's IRC 414(v) pool is deliberately not part of that test: it is sized from the very age in question, so it reads as empty exactly when the question is open.

vectors.name: 2026 a pension-linked emergency savings catch-up needs no prior-year FICA wages
vectors.description: IRC 414(v)(7)(A) requires that a catch-up contribution by a participant whose prior-year FICA wages from the sponsoring employer exceeded the indexed threshold be a designated Roth contribution, and this package asks for those wages so it can classify the catch-up. For a pension-linked emergency savings account the classification is already settled: IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account "for purposes of this title as a designated Roth account", so every contribution to it is a designated Roth contribution whatever the participant earned. The test has nothing left to decide, and demanding a fact that cannot change the answer would make an age-50 participant's account indeterminate for no statutory reason. This vector is the same scenario as the 401(k)-host catch-up case with the prior-year wage figure removed; the amount, its Roth character and the determinate status are unchanged.

vectors.name: 2026 a 457(b) plan-document deferral limit lowers the contributable amount but not the statutory maximum
vectors.description: IRC 457(b)(2) permits a plan to provide that the amount deferred for a year not exceed the lesser of the applicable dollar amount under IRC 457(e)(15) and 100 percent of the participant's includible compensation. Both terms are encoded law applied to supplied facts, so both belong in the statutory ceiling this package reports: with $200,000 of includible compensation the binding term is the $24,500 IRC 457(e)(15) figure Notice 2025-67 states for 2026. A $10,000 limit written into the plan document is neither — it is a restriction the sponsor chose — so it lowers what may actually be deferred to $10,000 while the statutory maximum stays $24,500. That is the line README draws for `statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution` and the line the qualified-plan path has always drawn; the IRC 457 path previously folded the plan-document limit into the reported figure and returned $10,000.

vectors.name: 2026 a 457(b) account with no plan-document limit is unchanged by the statutory-maximum split
vectors.description: The control for the preceding vector. Splitting the IRC 457(b)(2) ceiling into the statutory figure — the lesser of the IRC 457(e)(15) dollar amount and 100 percent of includible compensation — and the figure the plan document further restricts must change nothing where the plan document supplies no restriction: both are $24,500 for a 2026 participant with $200,000 of includible compensation, so the deferral, the pool draw and the reported statutory maximum all stay where they were. Without this vector the split could silently move the ordinary case while the plan-document case alone was watched.

vectors.name: 2026 a sponsor's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount caps the balance and not the year's deferrals
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) bars a contribution only to the extent it would cause the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions to exceed the lesser of clause (i)'s $2,600 for 2026 and clause (ii)'s amount set by the plan sponsor, here $1,000. Both clauses cap the same quantity -- a balance -- so the sponsor's amount is not a second, annual limit on deferrals, and the Department of Labor's PLESA guidance states that a plan may not impose a separate annual contribution limit on the account at all. $600 was contributed this year and withdrawn under the IRC 402A(e)(7) monthly withdrawal right, so the balance immediately before this allocation is $0 and the room is $1,000 - $0 = $1,000; the annual total reaches $600 + $1,000 = $1,600. Charging the year's $600 against the sponsor's $1,000 as well as against the balance would leave $400, stranding $600 of room the statute allows. The reported statutory maximum uses clause (i) only, because clause (ii) is a plan term: min($24,500 under IRC 402(g)(1) with no catch-up at age 36, $600 already contributed + ($2,600 - $0)) = $3,200.

vectors.name: 2026 an unwithdrawn balance leaves the sponsor's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) room correctly reduced
vectors.description: The control for the vector above, differing only in the supplied balance. Here the $600 contributed this year is still in the account, so the balance immediately before this allocation is $600 and IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) leaves $1,000 - $600 = $400 of room against the sponsor's clause (ii) amount. The annual total is $600 + $400 = $1,000, which is the sponsor's amount exactly, as it must be when nothing was withdrawn. Reading clause (ii) as a balance cap and reading it as an annual deferral limit give the same answer on these facts, which is why only the withdrawal case above distinguishes them; asserting both pins that the fix narrowed nothing. The statutory maximum again uses clause (i): min($24,500, $600 + ($2,600 - $600)) = $2,600.

vectors.name: 2026 a governmental 457(b)-hosted PLESA draws the IRC 457(e)(15) pool and not IRC 402(g)
vectors.description: IRC 402A(f)(1)(C) makes an eligible deferred compensation plan under IRC 457(b) of an IRC 457(e)(1)(A) employer a third applicable retirement plan that may hold a pension-linked emergency savings account. IRC 402(g)(3) enumerates elective deferrals exhaustively -- IRC 401(k) arrangements, IRC 402(h)(1)(B), IRC 403(b) salary-reduction annuities and IRC 408(p)(2)(A)(i) -- and no IRC 457(b) deferral is among them, so these contributions run against the IRC 457(e)(15) applicable dollar amount that IRC 457(b)(2)(A) imposes, $24,500 for 2026, and not against IRC 402(g)(1). IRC 402(g)(1) and IRC 457(e)(15) are the same figure in 2026, so no dollar amount can distinguish the two hosts; the pool identity can, and that is what is asserted here. IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) caps the participant-contribution portion of the balance at $2,600 for 2026, and the supplied balance is $0, so the room is the whole $2,600 and the base deferral takes all of it. IRC 457(b)(2)(B) caps the deferral at 100 percent of includible compensation, which at $200,000 does not bind.

vectors.name: 2026 a governmental 457(b)-hosted PLESA joins no IRC 415(c) group even when one is supplied
vectors.description: IRC 415(a)(1) reaches a trust forming part of a pension, profit-sharing or stock bonus plan, and IRC 415(a)(2) extends it to IRC 403(a) annuity plans, IRC 403(b) annuity contracts and IRC 408(k) simplified employee pensions. An IRC 457(b) plan is in neither list, so no annual-additions limitation reaches this account whatever the caller supplies. Both accounts here declare annualAdditionsGroupId 'g', and the 401(k) alone uses it: it defers the full IRC 402(g)(1) $24,500 against a $72,000 IRC 415(c)(1)(A) limitation. The PLESA's second pool is its own IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) room rather than that group, which is the positive form of the negative claim -- an index that would hold a 415c entry instead holds the room.

vectors.name: 2026 the two PLESA hosts share no pool with each other
vectors.description: IRC 402A(f)(1) makes three plan types an applicable retirement plan, and a participant may hold an emergency savings account in more than one. The limits they run against are different -- IRC 402(g)(1) for the IRC 401(a) trust, IRC 457(e)(15) for the governmental IRC 457(b) plan -- and IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps each account's own balance, since it speaks of 'the portion of the account balance'. So each takes its own $2,600 for 2026 and the participant contributes $5,200 across the two, which no single IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) balance cap could produce -- $5,200 is twice the 2026 figure. The $5,200 says nothing about the deferral limits, which are $24,500 apiece and could accommodate it either way; the pool identities asserted below are what separate those. The pool identities assert the separation directly: 402g:t against 457b:t, and one room pool per account.

vectors.name: 2023 a governmental 457(b)-hosted PLESA does not yet exist

The account is reported unavailable rather than given a zero limit.

vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 414(v) catch-up fills governmental 457(b) PLESA room the IRC 457(e)(15) pool cannot
vectors.description: IRC 414(v)(6)(A)(ii) makes an IRC 457(b) plan of an IRC 457(e)(1)(A) employer an applicable employer plan, and 26 CFR 1.414(v)-1(b)(1)(i) lists IRC 457(b)(2) among the limits a catch-up relieves. That is a limit on deferrals under the plan; IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) is a limit on an account balance. The two compose. The sibling governmental 457(b) account recognizes exactly $24,500 of includible compensation and defers all of it, so the shared IRC 457(e)(15) pool is spent and the PLESA's base deferral draws $0 from it. The $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) catch-up for 2026 is untouched, and the participant turns 56, so the whole $2,600 of IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) room is funded as a catch-up. It is Roth because IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account as a designated Roth account for purposes of the title. The statutory maximum is min($24,500 + $8,000, $0 already contributed + $2,600 of room) = $2,600.

vectors.name: 2026 the IRC 457(b)(3) last-three-years catch-up fills governmental 457(b) PLESA room
vectors.description: The catch-up this host has and the others do not. IRC 457(b)(3) raises 'the ceiling set forth in paragraph (2)' -- again a limit on deferrals under the plan and not on an account balance -- so it composes with IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) exactly as IRC 414(v) does. The sibling account spends the IRC 457(e)(15) pool, and the participant has $20,000 of unused deferrals from prior years, so the extra available under IRC 457(b)(3) is min($24,500, $20,000) = $20,000, which exceeds the $8,000 IRC 414(v) catch-up. IRC 457(e)(18) gives the participant the greater of the two and never their sum, and the engine reports which it chose. The $2,600 of room caps what that catch-up may actually fund. The statutory maximum is min($24,500 + $20,000, $0 + $2,600) = $2,600. The catch-up is Roth: IRC 457(b)(3) supplies the capacity, but IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account as a designated Roth account for purposes of the title, so a participant contribution to it is Roth whatever limitation it was made under. The two facts are independent, and the component records both -- special457RothCatchUp rather than special457CatchUp -- so the IRC 457(b)(3) pool is still the one seeded on a later calculation. The account reduces no Form W-2 box 1 wages and the whole $2,600 lands in the scenario's Roth total.

vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 457(b)(3) year needs no birth date, because IRC 414(v)(6)(C) removes the age catch-up
vectors.description: The same facts as the vector above but with no birth year supplied. IRC 414(v)(6)(C) provides that an IRC 457(b) plan is not an applicable employer plan for a participant for any year for which a *higher* limitation applies under IRC 457(b)(3), so the two limitations have to be compared -- and the comparison cannot be made against what this participant's age allows, because that is the unknown. It is made instead against the largest age-based catch-up 2026 could produce at any age: $11,250 under IRC 414(v)(2)(E) for ages 60 through 63, which exceeds the $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) figure. The $20,000 available under IRC 457(b)(3) here is above that, so IRC 457(b)(3) is the higher limitation however old the participant turns out to be, the age is not load-bearing, and the result stays determinate at $2,600. The sibling account's own silence about the missing birth date is pre-existing behaviour this vector does not assert.

vectors.name: 2026 a governmental 457(b) PLESA needs a birth date once a catch-up could reach its room
vectors.description: The mirror of the vector above, without the IRC 457(b)(3) eligibility that displaced the age-based catch-up. Whether it can be reached turns on an age that was not supplied, so the account is indeterminate rather than reporting a confident zero. The question is asked only here: where the base allocation had already spent the room, or where IRC 414(v)(6)(C) had removed the catch-up, no age could change the answer and none is demanded.

vectors.name: 2026 a sponsor's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount binds base and catch-up together on the 457(b) host
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps the balance at the lesser of clause (i)'s $2,600 and the plan sponsor's clause (ii) amount, here $1,000. Because it is one cap on one balance rather than a limit on each kind of contribution, the base deferral and the catch-up draw the same $1,000 of room: the sibling account has spent the IRC 457(e)(15) pool so the base takes $0, and the IRC 414(v) catch-up is then held to $1,000 rather than the $8,000 its own pool would allow. A model that applied the room as a base deferral limit would let the catch-up carry the balance past the sponsor's amount. Clause (ii) is a plan term, so the reported statutory maximum stays on clause (i): min($24,500 + $8,000, $0 + $2,600) = $2,600.

vectors.name: 2026 the sponsor's clause (ii) amount caps the balance on the 457(b) host too
vectors.description: The IRC 457(b) host mirror of the IRC 401(a) case: clause (ii) caps the same quantity clause (i) does, an account balance, so it is not a second annual limit on deferrals and the Department of Labor's PLESA guidance forbids the plan imposing one. $600 was contributed this year and withdrawn under the IRC 402A(e)(7) monthly withdrawal right, leaving $200 attributable to participant contributions immediately before this allocation, so the room against the sponsor's $1,000 is $800 and the annual total reaches $600 + $800 = $1,400. The participant is 36, so no catch-up can mask the base allocation. The statutory maximum uses clause (i): min($24,500, $600 + ($2,600 - $200)) = $3,000.

vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 457(b)(3) extra below the year's largest age catch-up still needs the birth date
vectors.description: The boundary the vector above sits on the other side of. IRC 457(b)(3) makes only $1,000 of unused prior deferrals available here, and $1,000 is below the $11,250 that IRC 414(v)(2)(E) would give a participant aged 60 through 63 in 2026. So IRC 457(b)(3) is not necessarily the higher limitation, IRC 414(v)(6)(C) does not remove the age-based catch-up, and the account is indeterminate. What is unknown is the *route* and not merely the amount: IRC 457(e)(18) picks between IRC 414(v) and IRC 457(b)(3), the two draw different pools, and on another host they would carry different tax treatment. So no catch-up is allocated under either heading and no catch-up pool is consumed -- reporting the $1,000 that IRC 457(b)(3) would certainly allow would put a floor in a field named for a maximum and file it under a statutory category these facts do not establish. Only the IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) room and the spent IRC 457(e)(15) pool are reported.

vectors.name: 2026 the same IRC 457(b)(3) facts with a known age take the larger IRC 414(v) catch-up instead
vectors.description: The control that shows the age in the vector above was load-bearing, and not merely unsupplied. IRC 457(e)(18) gives the greater of the two and never their sum, so the age-based catch-up is the one that applies and it funds the whole $2,600 of IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) room rather than $1,000 -- a different answer from the same inputs plus one birth year, which is why the missing one leaves the account indeterminate. It is Roth by IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i), and the special457CatchUp component is empty.

vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 457(b)(3) extra equal to the year's largest age catch-up still needs the birth date
vectors.description: IRC 414(v)(6)(C) removes the age-based catch-up only for a year in which a *higher* limitation applies under IRC 457(b)(3). Equal is not higher. The $11,250 of unused prior deferrals here exactly matches the IRC 414(v)(2)(E) figure for ages 60 through 63 in 2026, so IRC 414(v) remains available and which route applies still turns on the age. The dollar amounts the two routes would fund happen to coincide, but the routes do not: they draw different pools and record different components, which is why an equal amount cannot be treated as settling the question. vectors.name: 2026 the same equal IRC 457(b)(3) amount with a known age of 61 takes the IRC 414(v) route

IRC 457(e)(18) gives the greater of the two, and on a tie the age-based route applies because IRC 414(v)(6)(C) has not displaced it. The $2,600 of IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) room is funded from the IRC 414(v) pool, whose limit reads $11,250 rather than the $8,000 of IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i), and is recorded as employeeRothCatchUp rather than as an IRC 457(b)(3) amount. vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 457(b)(3) catch-up to a Roth governmental 457(b) is Roth, not pre-tax
